World.title: License plate cameras are tracking drivers everywhere
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

One minute, you are driving to the grocery store. The next, a camera above the road photographs your car and adds the sighting to a searchable database. You probably will not hear a click or see a flash. In fact, you may never notice the camera mounted on a pole near the intersection.

Automated license plate readers have quietly spread across the country. As of our reporting, the open-source DeFlock map displayed about 119,000 readers across the United States. DeFlock is a community-powered project that maps reported camera locations using public submissions and data from OpenStreetMap. Because the map relies partly on crowdsourced information, it may miss some cameras or include locations that have changed.

Flock Safety cameras account for about 83% of the mapped total. California has the largest number of mapped readers, with more than 16,000. Major clusters appear around Los Angeles and the Bay Area. Police say the cameras help locate stolen cars and vehicles connected to serious crimes.

FLOCK SURVEILLANCE SPREADS ACROSS THE SOUTH AS RED-STATE LAWMAKERS SEEK TO AX '1984'-STYLE TRACKING TOOLS

However, privacy advocates warn that the same network can reveal where ordinary people travel throughout the day. Each sighting can include a vehicle's plate number, appearance, location and the time it passed the camera. Flock says its system can search by plate, vehicle type and visible features.

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

Why license plate cameras are appearing everywhere

Automated license plate readers, also known as ALPRs or LPRs, have become common tools for police departments. Businesses and homeowners associations can also install them. The rules can vary depending on who owns the camera and who gets access to the data.

The cameras often appear on poles near streets, intersections and neighborhood entrances. Some have solar panels attached to the pole. As a car passes, the camera takes a photograph. Software reads the license plate and turns the image into a searchable record. CyberGuy previously found that license plate cameras are also scanning vehicles at some Home Depot and Lowe's parking lots.

Flock Safety has become one of the largest vendors in this market. Its cameras connect to a cloud-based system where authorized customers can review vehicle sightings. Unlike red-light cameras, these readers generally focus on identifying vehicles. They typically do not issue traffic tickets. Still, every passing vehicle can enter the database. The driver does not need to face suspicion or have any connection to an investigation.

What license plate cameras capture about your car

A reader begins with your license plate number. However, the record can include much more than the characters printed on the plate. The system records a vehicle's make and model. It can also note the color and body type.

Visible features may become searchable as well. These can include a roof rack, bumper sticker or missing hubcap. The record also includes the camera location and a timestamp. Together, those details show where the vehicle appeared and when it passed. Flock says its license plate reader system focuses on vehicles rather than faces. The company also says its LPR cameras exclude facial recognition and biometric identification.

Your daily drive can become searchable data

A single camera sighting may reveal little about your day. Several sightings can start to form a pattern. For example, a vehicle that appears near the same house each evening may reveal where someone lives. Another record could show a visit to a medical provider.

A license plate can also connect a car to information held by a state motor vehicle agency. That connection can help investigators identify the registered owner. Authorized personnel can search for a complete plate number. They may also search using a partial plate or vehicle description.

A department looking for a dark SUV with a roof rack could receive several possible matches. Investigators would then need to confirm which vehicle they want. That search ability can save time during an urgent case. Meanwhile, it also gives agencies access to information about drivers who have done nothing wrong.

Where the license plate camera network is growing

California leads the country with more than 16,000 mapped readers, according to an analysis of DeFlock data. Florida followed with 7,169 cameras. Georgia had 7,046. Illinois had 5,822. The concentration becomes clearer when the figures are compared with road mileage. San Francisco County ranked third nationwide with 1,196 cameras per 1,000 road miles. Only New York County and Kings County ranked higher.

In Southern California, Orange County ranked No. 33 nationwide. It had 184 cameras per 1,000 road miles. Los Angeles County ranked No. 59 with 143 cameras per 1,000 miles.

However, DeFlock cannot provide a complete camera inventory. The open-source project relies on public reports and data from other sources. As a result, populated communities may have more markers because more people submit camera locations. Rural areas may appear less covered even when readers exist there. A missing marker cannot guarantee that a road has no camera. Likewise, some mapped locations may need updates after a camera moves or disappears.

How police use license plate camera data

Police departments can place license plates connected to stolen vehicles on a hotlist. They may also add cars linked to active investigations. When a camera detects a matching plate, the system can alert officers. That may help them locate a stolen car or find a missing person's vehicle. Investigators can also search earlier sightings. Those records may show where a vehicle appeared before or after an incident. However, an automated alert still requires human verification.

A recent LAPD review examined more than 210 million plate scans over two months. The system incorrectly flagged 161 plates as stolen. Yet not every incorrect alert led to a police encounter. During the same period, 337 alerts helped officers recover stolen vehicles. Those results show both the investigative value and the risk of an incorrect match.

Why privacy advocates are raising alarms

License plate readers collect information from millions of vehicles. Most belong to people with no connection to a crime. Privacy advocates say connected camera networks can create a detailed driving history without requiring a warrant. They also worry about access by agencies far from the community that installed the camera.

Those concerns have already affected ordinary drivers. CyberGuy reported on a Colorado woman who was wrongly accused after Flock camera records linked her truck to the area of a porch theft. She had to gather Google Location Timeline data, vehicle camera footage and other evidence to prove where she had been. Police later voided the summons and dropped the case.

California restricts where ALPR data can go

California law limits how local law enforcement agencies share automated license plate reader information. The state prohibits local agencies from giving ALPR data to federal authorities or out-of-state agencies. State officials say the information must remain within California.

However, allegations of improper sharing have raised questions about whether every agency follows those restrictions. California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued the city of El Cajon in October 2025. His office accused the city of sharing ALPR data with more than 100 out-of-state law enforcement agencies.

In January 2026, Bonta asked a court to order the city to stop the sharing. The case remained part of California's effort to enforce its ALPR privacy laws. The dispute highlights a gap between written policy and technical enforcement. A rule may prohibit sharing, but the system also needs controls that block unauthorized access.

THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

LAPD pauses Flock access after agreement expires

The Los Angeles Police Department entered a three-year operating agreement with Flock Safety in 2023. The arrangement covered access to data from 138 pole-mounted cameras across the city. The agreement expired on July 11, 2026. LAPD allowed it to lapse while officials addressed concerns involving data ownership, privacy and security. The department also wanted clearer limits on how Flock could store, share and use information collected by the cameras.

The 138 cameras continued operating after the agreement ended. However, LAPD employees no longer had regular access to the data they collected. That information remained stored in the cloud and could become available to investigators if the city finalizes a new agreement. Police officials began negotiating proposed terms with stronger safeguards. Under those terms, the city would retain ownership of every image, record and piece of metadata captured by the cameras.

Flock would also be prohibited from selling, publishing or sharing the information with outside organizations. In addition, the company could not use the data for commercial purposes or to train artificial intelligence systems. As of our reporting, LAPD and Flock had reportedly not finalized a replacement agreement, and talks are believed to be ongoing.

LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell called the technology a valuable investigative tool. Still, he said the department needed to use it responsibly. The dispute shows how quickly a camera program can raise difficult questions about control and oversight. Those questions become harder to resolve after a large network has already begun collecting information.

What Flock Safety says about driver privacy

Flock rejects claims that its license plate readers continuously track a vehicle. The company says each camera captures a vehicle at one specific location. However, authorized agencies can search separate sightings stored within the system.

Flock says its default retention period lasts 30 days. Customers may choose a different period based on local laws or contract terms. The company also says customers control their information and sharing settings. According to Flock, every search is connected to a specific account and recorded in an activity log.

However, access questions can become more complicated when public-records laws enter the picture. CyberGuy previously reported that a Washington judge ruled Flock license plate reader images can qualify as public records, even when a private company stores the files for a city. The decision did not mean every driver record would automatically become public. However, it showed that using an outside vendor may not remove government surveillance data from state transparency laws.

Flock also says it does not sell customer data or use facial recognition with its LPR cameras. It says automated deletion and annual security audits help confirm that agencies follow their selected retention periods. Those safeguards address part of the privacy debate. Yet their effectiveness depends on how each customer configures the system and reviews employee activity.

What license plate cameras mean for you

You may never receive a notification when a license plate camera records your vehicle. Still, you can learn more about the readers operating around your community.

Start with the DeFlock map

Check DeFlock at deflock.org for reported cameras near your home and regular driving routes. Remember that public submissions help build the map. Therefore, it may contain gaps or outdated locations. Look for cameras mounted high on narrow poles. A nearby solar panel can also signal a roadside reader.

Local policies reveal retention rules

Search your city or police department website for its ALPR policy. The policy may explain how long the department keeps vehicle records. It should also describe the types of investigations that allow a search. Do not assume every agency uses Flock's 30-day default. Contracts and local rules can set a shorter or longer retention period.

Outside access deserves a closer look

Find out whether other departments can search your community's camera data. A city may have strict internal rules while sharing access with a much larger network. That wider access can make local safeguards harder to evaluate. Look for an agency transparency portal if one exists. You can also request a list of connected departments from your city.

Watch contracts before cameras multiply

City council agendas often reveal proposed camera purchases before installation begins. Search meeting documents for terms such as "ALPR," "automated license plate reader" or "Flock Safety." Contract documents may show how many cameras the city plans to install. They can also explain who will own the records. Public meetings give residents a chance to ask questions before officials approve a larger network.

Find out who checks for misuse

Ask who reviews searches for possible abuse. Audit logs offer limited protection when nobody checks them. You should also find out what happens after an employee violates the policy. Departments should explain whether they suspend access or begin an investigation. Strong consequences can discourage personal searches. They also show whether an agency treats its privacy rules seriously.

Kurt's key takeaways

License plate readers can help police find a stolen vehicle or develop leads after a serious crime. That explains why departments, businesses and homeowners associations continue installing them. Still, these cameras record everyday drivers who have no connection to an investigation. A series of sightings can reveal where you go and when, even though the camera never captures your face. The Colorado case shows what can happen when a camera record points police toward the wrong person. Meanwhile, the Washington ruling raises another concern because some images held for a city may qualify as public records. Flock says customers control their data and can review searches through activity logs. Those protections depend on departments limiting access, checking for misuse and enforcing their own policies. LAPD's decision to pause access after its agreement expired shows that privacy concerns can slow a major camera program. However, the ongoing talks suggest the technology will remain part of the public safety debate. Before more cameras appear, your community deserves clear answers about who can search the records, how long the data stays available and what happens when someone abuses access.

Would you accept license plate cameras throughout your community if police said they helped solve crimes, or has this type of tracking already gone too far? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

FAUCI PLEADS FIFTH WITH 'ZERO LEGAL JUSTIFICATION' AS CRITICS ERUPT AND DEMAND CONTEMPT CHARGES

We will examine the physical and monetary harms to Floridians that may have resulted from his deceptions and determine whether his conduct exposes him to liability under state law," Uthmeier's statement concluded.

Uthmeier cited revelations published by Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., which revealed internal notes Fauci wrote on government computers during his time at NIAID.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

The internal notes, which Paul and others have taken to referring to as Fauci's "diary," suggest Fauci appeared to publicly overstate the death rate from COVID-19 compared to what he wrote privately.

"[Former CDC Director] Tom Frieden called me this AM and we discussed various aspects of the outbreak," Fauci wrote on Feb. 8, 2020.

World.title: Kamala Harris' new $8M mansion is in a neighborhood with virtually no Black residents
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Despite a career-long commitment to combatting racial disparities in housing and touting the importance of living among Black people, former Vice President Kamala Harris’s new California mansion is situated in a neighborhood with virtually no racial diversity.

Harris’s new 4,000-square-foot property, which reports indicate she acquired for $8.15 million, is located in the exclusive seaside community of Point Dume and includes ocean views, multiple wine fridges, private golf greens and enough parking to accommodate five vehicles.

Point Dume is situated entirely within Census tract 8004.08, which the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey estimated was just 0.2% Black and roughly 94% White as of 2019.

Harris's choice of neighborhood may surprise longtime observers given past comments she has made about the importance of living among other Black Americans.

KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY

"When you’re at (a historically black college or university), and especially one with the size and with the history of Howard University — and also in the context of also being in D.C., which was known forever as being ‘Chocolate City’ — it just becomes about you understanding that there is a whole world of people who are like you," Harris told a Washington Post reporter in 2019, reflecting on her experience growing up in primarily White social circles then attending a historically Black college in a predominantly African American city.

"It was more, for me, about the numerosity than it was the diversity, I grew up in a community where there were many representations of diversity," she added. "Going to Howard, there were so many (Black people)! And they’re all in your age group, in your phase of life."

Now, however, Harris has chosen to put roots down in a community that at least one group has accused of trying to keep their beaches closed off to minorities.

CHICAGO SUBURB LOCALS HOPE REPARATIONS ADDRESSES 'AFFORDABILITY PRESSURES' AS BLACK POPULATION DWINDLES

"Despite the veneer of a laid back community of surfers who are one with nature, there are barriers to access that keep most BIPOC people away," a pair of non-White surfers wrote in a 2025 review of Harris’s new neighborhood.

Harris spent a sizable portion of her career working to tear down similar barriers.

HARRIS STOPS IN KEY PRESIDENTIAL PRIMARY STATE AFTER LEAVING DOOR WIDE OPEN TO 2028 RUN

In 2012, as California’s attorney general, for instance, she joined a Supreme Court brief arguing that the Fair Housing Act can be enforced when policies have a "disparate impact" across different racial groups, even if the policies themselves are racially neutral.

As a presidential candidate, she proposed $100 billion in assistance for families in historically redlined communities and as vice president she promoted the Biden administration’s efforts to combat racial bias in home appraisals.

During Harris’s 2020 presidential campaign, she faced questions about the authenticity of her African American identity due to her Indian and Jamaican heritage and upbringing in affluent, primarily White areas. The attacks resurfaced in 2024, when then-candidate Donald Trump accused Harris of using her Black identity for political gain.

Harris caught flak during the 2024 campaign for identifying with Oakland, California, even though she spent most of her childhood growing up in Berkeley, California, which was significantly less racially diverse. As a teenager, she moved to Montreal, another predominantly White city, with her mother.

Doug Emhoff, Harris' husband, is also White.

FIRST ON FOX: Florida Republican Sen. Ashley Moody introduced a bill targeting the Washington, D.C. public school system in a push to prioritize patriotism in the nation’s capital, Fox News Digital has learned.

The PLEDGE Act proposal would require teachers to feature the American Flag in their classrooms, and for administrators to provide students the opportunity to recite the Pledge of Allegiance every day.

"Currently, there are schools in Washington, D.C., the nation’s capital, that do not display our flag or set aside time for students to recite the Pledge of Allegiance, but they do teach them to be activists," claims the press release shared with Fox News Digital.

FAR-LEFT ACTIVIST CONFERENCE AT TEACHERS UNION HQ RAISES CLASSROOM CONCERNS

In a city where Pride flags and progressive causes are prominently displayed across the district, some conservatives say patriotic symbols like the American Flag have taken a back seat in schools — fueling concerns about how civic values are being taught to the next generations of Americans.

"Radicals want to teach kids to be ashamed of the United States of America and how to be activists instead. We should be teaching kids why America is worth loving, and most importantly, the principles and values that make America worth defending," said Sen. Moody in the release.

Over 40 states have varying Pledge requirements in their schools — but not in the nation’s capital.

"My PLEDGE Act helps restore pride in our nation by reminding students every day of the freedom, responsibilities, and blessings that come with being an American, and the sacrifices made for our flag and everything it represents," Moody said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.

BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

The bill comes amid a mayoral race in D.C., where socialist candidate Janeese Lewis George is the frontrunner. This continues a trend in the nationwide rise of the far-left Democratic Socialist of America (DSA) movement, which often spouts anti-American rhetoric.

The DSA platform, which aims to appeal to younger voters, wants to replace free-market capitalism with social ownership. It also pushes for major constitutional changes, like abolishing the Electoral College and expanding voting rights for noncitizens.

Younger Americans are significantly less likely to express strong national pride than older generations, with just 41% of Generation Z saying they are extremely or very proud to be American, according to a June 2025 Gallup poll.

The same poll says 58% of U.S. adults say they are "extremely" or "very" proud to be American, the lowest level the pollsters have recorded since it began asking the question in 2001.

DEMS PUT ON BLAST OVER POLL THAT SHOWS RECORD-LOW PATRIOTISM IN US: 'TEAR OUR SOCIETY APART'

The DC Public School (DCPS) curriculum calls for students to learn more progressive politics, from studying Harvey Milk to learning how the LGBTQ+ community has shaped and defined the Washington, D.C. community.

For example, 5th grade social studies standards in the district require students to analyze the rise of queer culture during the Black Renaissance and also require students to compare the experiences of LGBTQ+ service members returning to the U.S. after World War II, according to their 2023 Social Study Standards.

During President Donald Trump's second term, his administration restored patriotic symbols to the nation's capital by installing two large American flags on the White House grounds and removing the "Black Lives Matter" street mural on the plaza just blocks from the executive residence.

World.title: 'Hot seat rankings' for all 16 SEC coaches as beginning of 2026 college football season draws nearer
World.content:
At the beginning of every college football season, there are always a few questions that are on every fan's mind.

One of which is "who looks like they can win it all every season," but since I already addressed that earlier this week, I'm here to tackle the second most popular question: which coaches are on the hot seat heading into fall?

More specifically, I wanted to look at every coach from the SEC and give them a "hot seat ranking" based on their job security in 2026.

PERCEPTION IS REALITY, AND THE SEC NEEDS TO START WINNING AGAIN BEFORE IT CONTINUES TO PUFF OUT ITS CHEST

I will be lumping all 16 SEC coaches into one of five categories that should give everyone an idea of where these guys stand before the start of the season.

We have a lot to get to, so let's get this hot seat party started.

New Coaches: Alex Golesh (Auburn), Pete Golding (Ole Miss), Lane Kiffin (LSU), Jon Sumrall (Florida), Ryan Silverfield (Arkansas), Will Stein (Kentucky)

The SEC has six "new" coaches among its ranks in 2026, and the reason I put a heavy set of quotations around that word is because some of these guys have already been coaches in the conference.

Obviously, Lane Kiffin was previously at Ole Miss for six years and even had an infamous stop in Knoxville for one season to coach the Tennessee Vols, but if we want to get technical, the Rebels have a "returning" SEC coach of their own in Pete Golding.

The colorful successor to Kiffin in Oxford guided Ole Miss to the College Football Playoff semifinals in 2025, but 2026 will be his first full season, so I'm including him here.

None of these guys are getting fired in their first season, so they earned themselves a ranking almost completely removed from the rest of the guys on this list.

THREE SEC WIN TOTALS YOU SHOULD ABSOLUTELY POUNCE ON BEFORE THE 2026 COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON BEGINS

Sure, if Kiffin has a first-year implosion and finishes 6-6, he will certainly be sitting on a blazing hot seat coming into 2027, but no one else is even close to that talk right now.

Enjoy it, men. Odds are you will never feel this secure in your job again.

Sitting On A Block Of Dry Ice: Kirby Smart (Georgia), Clark Lea (Vanderbilt)

The seat can't get much colder than this, and ironically enough, these two coaches sit on opposite ends of the royalty spectrum in the SEC.

Kirby Smart has earned every bit of the job security he has going for him, as the Georgia Bulldogs head coach enters year 11 of his storied career in Athens.

In 2021, the man delivered a national championship 40 years in the making to a starving fanbase then followed it up with another the very next year just for good measure.

Though Georgia fans aren't thrilled with their recent lack of CFP success, the Dawgs are still reigning SEC champs and look like the favorites to win the league again in 2026, so Kirby's seat is ice cold.

For Clark Lea, just the fact that he had Vandy of all programs knocking on the door of the Playoff last season means his seat couldn't get any colder.

For crying out loud, the man won ten games at Vanderbilt, something no coach has ever done in program history.

When you couple that with the fact that guys like Diego Pavia, Eli Stowers, and a smattering of offensive linemen aren't in Nashville anymore, fans rightly expect the Commodores to take a step back in '26, cooling the seat even more for Lea.

Vandy could go 2-10 this year and I still don't think Clark Lea will be packing his bags. Now THAT'S job security.

Lawn Chair On A Spring Morning: Mike Elko (Texas A&M), Eli Drinkwitz (Missouri), Steve Sarkisian (Texas)

These three coaches are sitting on some pretty cool seats, all things considered.

While the situations aren't perfect, they can't get much better for at least two of the three names in this category.

Mike Elko led the Texas A&M Aggies to an 11-win season and a Playoff berth, and for a fanbase desperate to shed those pre-World War II championship taunts, it feels like a step in the right direction.

When you pair the winning with A&M's historic recruiting class that is brewing for 2027, Elko is as cool as a cucumber.

The same goes for Eli Drinkwitz, who experienced a bit of a step back in 2025, but still won eight games and has things trending up in Columbia.

Drinkwitz earned a massive extension after being courted by a few big boy job openings like Florida and Penn State, and while that doesn't always guarantee job security (as I'll explain later), it is a nice bonus to help keep the seat cool.

Steve Sarkisian is the outlier here, as I almost put him in the next category.

I don't believe Sark is in any danger of losing his job, hence the cool seat, but the expectations for this season are so high that, should he fail to deliver, we could be having an entirely different conversation 365 days from now.

But that hasn't happened yet, so for now, Sark and Texas are rolling and 2025 should be considered just a minor blip on the radar.

Heated Seat In A Luxury Sedan: Brent Venables (Oklahoma), Jeff Lebby (Mississippi State), Josh Heupel (Tennessee), Kalen DeBoer (Alabama)

Things start warming up in this category; perhaps these coaches are starting to sweat through their team-issued polos.

No coach in this category is in any immediate danger of being fired during the 2026 season, but a bad start could really raise those temperatures in a hurry.

For three of the four coaches here, it's all about expectations.

DeBoer, Heupel, and Venables have all been solid to very good throughout most of their tenures at their respective schools.

The problem is that all three are at programs that demand excellence.

DeBoer in particular is standing in the shadow of perhaps the biggest giant to ever coach in the Southeastern Conference, and although he just signed an extension to stay in Tuscaloosa, having an empty trophy case with regard to SEC and national championships is starting to make the natives very restless.

Another season without a deep Playoff run could send DeBoer packing.

Heupel's rope is a touch longer than Venables', given that this year is supposed to be a ramp-up for what should be a loaded 2027 roster in Knoxville, but the Vols have zero Playoff wins entering year six of his tenure.

Finally, Jeff Lebby probably deserves to be in the tier above this one, especially since the Bulldogs were a barren wasteland of talent when he came to town and they were a few plays away from potentially being an eight or nine-win team last year.

But another sub-.500 season will almost certainly give even the most patient fans and boosters in Starkville a reason to start looking for the exit door of the Lebby era.

Recliner At The Mouth Of An Active Volcano: Shane Beamer (South Carolina)

I wrote an article last month about how you could make the argument that Shane Beamer's seat is the hottest in the country, and that includes a man by the name of Mike Norvell.

Beamer's seat is radioactive heading into the 2026 season, and much of that has to do with that dirty word, "expectations," again.

South Carolina was a dark-horse candidate to make the College Football Playoff last season and ended up face-planting to the tune of a 4-8 campaign.

A similar 4-8 season for a CFP hopeful in Florida cost Billy Napier his job, so another subpar record in 2026 could spell doom for Beamer and co.

The Gamecocks have an incendiary talent at quarterback in LaNorris Sellers, a freak athlete at wide receiver in Nyck Harbor, and an all-conference selection and future first-round draft pick at edge rusher in Dylan Stewart, so the pieces are in place, at least in theory, to have a good bounce-back year.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Anything less than 8-4 is probably a massive disappointment in Columbia, and I could honestly see Beamer being shown the door if South Carolina isn't at least 4-2 by the time their bye week rolls around.

The SEC is a cutthroat league, and Beamer could end up being the latest casualty before the season is even over.

World.title: Tomi Adeyemi says she left film set of adaption of her ‘Children of Blood and Bone’ in tears
World.content:
Author Tomi Adeyemi, whose novel “Children of Blood and Bone” is being made into a movie, said in a TikTok video that she left the set of the book’s film adaptation in tears.

Throughout the video, posted Wednesday, an emotional Adeyemi referenced suffering on the set but did not provide any details of what transpired.

In the video, the author said she wouldn’t speak about “everything that I also suffered through, or endured, to make the adaptation a reality.”

Instead, she said she was only going to speak about “what happened after I left that set of my own film adaptation hyperventilating and sobbing, and there are many witnesses so it’s not really a secret.”

“I came back to America and suffered such severe somatic pain and so many panic attacks and I knew it was so bad that I would never ever be able to watch this film and I made peace with that,” she said.

“But as it is being marketed,” she said, referencing the film’s trailer, which dropped on Tuesday, “and as I am still being antagonized behind the scenes, which is where I hoped all of this would stay, it’s become apparent to me that that reality needs to at least be made known so that you guys can understand how this film, which I worked on to make it a little better for us to be alive, is also the worst thing I have ever had to live through, and I don’t wish to speak on it anymore.”

Adeyemi co-wrote the movie’s screenplay. She has previously spoken about how she will never watch the film because of experiences she had on set.

The high profile Paramount film is set for release in January. It is being directed by acclaimed filmmaker Gina Prince-Bythewood and has a star-studded cast that includes Cynthia Erivo, Idris Elba and Viola Davis.

NBC News has contacted Adeyemi for comment and more context on her allegations. Paramount and Prince-Bythewood were also contacted and did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Earlier this month, Adeyemi posted a now-deleted TikTok that appeared to show screenshots of a group chat including both her and actor Amandla Stenberg, who stars in “Children of Blood and Bone.”

“Do not ever use my name in an interview or video again. Do not text me. Do not call me,” Adeyemi wrote in the group chat, according to the L.A. Times. The screenshot also appeared to show that Adeyemi blocked Stenberg.

Neither has spoken publicly about a feud. But Stenberg has faced backlash over her casting as Princess Amari in the film adaptation due to allegations of colorism, Variety reported.

“I am four months into training for ‘Children of Blood and Bone’ and I am getting my ass whooped,” Stenberg said in a TikTok video posted last year that has since been deleted, according to Variety.

“I want everyone to know that this is important to me, and I think about it with every choice that I make. I would never navigate my career blindly, not thinking about my skin tone or the space I occupy. I would never go after a role I didn’t feel was right for me,” she said in the deleted video, which appeared to address the colorism allegations.

“I want to see all skin tones represented in media,” she said. “I know that colorism is an insidious system that relentlessly impacts every facet of entertainment.”

A representative for Stenberg did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Adeyemi, in the Wednesday video, said the allegations were “not a secret to the people involved,” without mentioning who those people were.

“It’s a reality that I’ve had to live with for about a year and a half and everyone involved, at least at the highest level, has been made aware of this reality and they haven’t done anything to make it better,” she said. “If anything, they’ve only antagonized me, and I accept that, but I also accept if I don’t say something, I think it’s just gonna be worse.”

She said she chose to speak out because “being silent about it is making the pain a lot worse.”

“Please understand I never want to hear about this project again,” Adeyemi continued, while also acknowledging that it may not be possible to stop speaking on the issue, as she has a public presence and the movie is a global project.

“I don’t have anything to say about the people who made it. I do not care anymore. I am trying to move on,” she said. “This video might make it worse, but I don’t know how it can be any worse, so I’m just going to share that and let it live.”

World.title: Ben Affleck wins $1 million for charity on ‘Who Wants To Be a Millionaire’
World.content:
Ben Affleck was overcome with glee the moment he won “Who Wants To Be a Millionaire,” jumping up to hug his partner, “Jeopardy!” champion Jamie Ding.

Affleck and Ding made it to the final round on Wednesday’s episode of the ABC game show, hosted by Jimmy Kimmel, where they faced a question about turkeys pardoned by U.S. presidents. The duo had to deduce which names did not belong to pardoned turkeys.

“So we’re gonna say D, Spaghtetti and Meatball?” Ding said after deliberations.

“Yeah,” Affleck nodded.

It took a beat before the answer was revealed, leaving Affleck and Ding looking stressed about their choice. But the chime indicating they chose correctly rang out and both men jumped to their feet for an excited hug.

Ben Affleck and Jamie Ding in "Who Wants To Be a Millionaire." Eric McCandless / Disney

The two men were playing for charity. Their prize winnings will be donated to the Eastern Congo Initiative, a nonprofit co-founded by Affleck in 2010 to support Congolese communities.

Affleck spoke on the game show about how he has spent the last 15 years working with the organization.

“And right now, of course, as I’m sure most people know, there’s an Ebola crisis there,” Affleck said. “And so this is in large part designed to try to relieve that, contain the spread of Ebola.”

The Oscar-winning actor, director and writer was lucky to have Ding as a partner, as the former “Jeopardy!” contestant had a historic run on that trivia show. Ding managed a 31-game streak, landing fifth on the list of all-time “Jeopardy!” winners.

Current host Ken Jennings still holds the top spot with 74 consecutive wins.

It’s unclear when “Who Wants To Be a Millionaire” was filmed, but Affleck’s win was aired a year after his best friend, Matt Damon, appeared on the show. The “Good Will Hunting” co-writer won $1 million for his own charity, Water.org, after being paired up with Jennings.

Affleck’s episode also aired a week after news broke that his mother died following a pancreatic cancer diagnosis. Christopher Affleck, or Chris, died on June 2, but her obituary appeared in The Boston Globe last week.

It said that her greatest wish was to see her grandson’s high school graduation, which she attended two days before her death.

World.title: Trump threatens to pull Todd Blanche’s AG nomination until after GOP holdouts leave office
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Thursday threatened to withdraw Todd Blanche’s nomination to be attorney general until two Republican senators who have expressed concerns about Blanche leave office in January.

“I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office,” he said in a Thursday post to Truth Social.

The Senate Judiciary Committee postponed a vote to advance Blanche’s nomination over objections from Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina. A single Republican no vote would mean the nomination fails to advance.

The pair have expressed hesitancy to support Blanche over concerns with Trump’s settlement with the Internal Revenue Service regarding the leak of his tax returns.

Responding to Trump’s post, Cornyn said on X that the president “is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis.”

Tillis slammed Trump’s proposal as “about as politically tone deaf a posture as I have seen in this administration.”

He argued that the move would give journalists and Democrats “gold to mine between now and the election.” The North Carolina senator also said that Trump could “roll the dice” on the Senate confirmation process once he and Cornyn are out of office, but added, “it’s all on him.”

With midterm elections less than 100 days away, it’s unclear whether Republicans will still control the Senate come January. If Democrats flip control of the Senate, they could block Blanche’s nomination.

“What I’m focused on is the main thing, and the main thing is the 1776 fund needs to go away, or they’re going to hang this yoke around our candidates’ necks, and rightly so,” Tillis said.

“I believe the only logical conclusion I can draw from this setback is that, in fact, there is somebody who wants to enable it at the right time,” he added. “That’s unacceptable.”

As part of the IRS lawsuit settlement, the Justice Department created a $1.776 “anti-weaponization” fund. The DOJ backtracked after bipartisan criticism, but Cornyn and Tillis are pushing for the Justice Department to formalize the verbal commitment in writing.

The lawmakers are also asking that the Justice Department narrow part of the settlement that provided Trump, his family members and companies with protections against IRS audits.

Tillis told reporters on Thursday that he believed Blanche was “trying to fulfill the commitment he made in the hearing” but that someone was “in the way.”

“Todd Blanche is negotiating in good faith, but it’s clear that the approval to get this done is above his pay grade, and we just need to get to that pay grade,” Tillis said. “I don’t believe it’s the president. I got to get to finance guys.”

Cornyn expressed a similar view, telling reporters that he believed “if this were just between me and Todd Blanche, we would have worked this out.”

“But apparently, he’s getting some pushback from higher-ups at the White House,” he said. “I don’t know who, but this doesn’t need to be this hard.”

Cornyn said that the Justice Department was reluctant to change the formal settlement documents, so his team instead proposed “some additional paper” that would commit Blanche to his sworn Judiciary Committee testimony.

If the Justice Department agreed, Cornyn said his concerns would be satisfied. During his congressional testimony, Blanche testified the weaponization fund “is dead,” the audit protections do not extend beyond the parties to the lawsuit, and the settlement “doesn’t cover any government entity except the IRS.”

Inside the White House, a senior administration official said that people familiar with conversations involving Cornyn accused the senator of moving the goalposts, canceling meetings and refusing to communicate with the department.

Cornyn lost his primary election to the Trump-endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and Tillis, who has clashed with Trump repeatedly, is retiring at the end of his term.

Trump took credit for the pair leaving office at the end of their terms, saying in his post that their “political careers have been ended by my action.”

World.title: Megan Moroney tearfully cancels Denver show mid-performance over illness
World.content:
County music star Megan Moroney was forced to reschedule her Denver concert after singing just three songs on Tuesday night over an illness that affected her performance.

Ball Arena confirmed the cancelation in a statement that said Moroney was “unable to continue” and that the venue would provide updates when available. Videos from concertgoers also showed that the “Tennessee Orange” singer addressed the crowd before announcing the show was over.

“This is obviously the last thing I would ever want to do, but I’m obviously extremely sick,” Moroney said, according to multiple videos posted online. “I thought I did everything to make myself better and then obviously two songs in, I just can’t play this show tonight. I will make it up to you guys — I absolutely promise I’ll be back.”

Moroney added that she wanted to give her fans the show they deserved before saying she would probably go back to cry in her dressing room. Her voice sounded hoarse and it seemed she was choking back tears as she apologized to the crowd.

In a statement posted to her Instagram story, Moroney announced that the show would be rescheduled for August 27. Fans who are unable to make the new date would be given full refunds, according to NBC affiliate KUSA.

“I never ever will give you guys a show that is not 100% and I knew that I was not capable of giving that to you tonight,” she wrote.

The country star is not the first to have to pivot mid-show due to illness this summer. Lionel Richie rescheduled dates on his tour with Earth, Wind & Fire in June after feeling unwell during their opening night in in St. Paul, Minnesota.

Richie addressed the crowd at the time, telling them that he felt dizzy during his performance of “Dancing on the Ceiling,” NBC affiliate KARE reported at the time. He said that he’s learned over the years to sit down if he’s feeling dizzy, which he did during the song.

“Now, I want you to know that’s the first time in the history of ‘Dancing on the Ceiling’ I’ve done it sitting down,” Richie said. “That’s a bad sign, that’s a bad sign, y’all.”

Live Nation released a statement shortly after that the tour’s dates in Chicago and Pittsburgh would be postponed due to doctor’s advice that the 77-year-old “rest and return to full health.”

Jon Bon Jovi was performing at New York City’s Madison Square Garden when he suddenly started struggling during “Livin’ on a Prayer.” The lead singer of Train, Pat Monahan, stepped in to help finish the song. Monahan was at the venue to serve as a surprise guest.

A representative for Bon Jovi told NBC New York that the New Jersey native was struggling with a sinus infection. The show was canceled after roughly an hour and a half.

Bon Jovi apologized to the crowd and promised he would find a way to make it up to them, NBC New York reported.

“Don’t throw away your ticket stubs, I’m gonna figure something out, OK?” he said. “Just hold onto it, we’ll figure out how to reschedule.”

World.title: Trump says he may pull Blanche's nomination until 2 Senate critics leave office
World.content:
Washington — President Trump on Thursday said he has "no objection" to withdrawing Todd Blanche's nomination for attorney general until Republican Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina leave office in January, as their concerns have effectively placed Blanche's nomination process on hold.

Cornyn in particular has demanded that the Justice Department and Blanche formally put in writing that the DOJ's "anti-weaponization fund" won't return, and has demanded changes to the president's personal IRS settlement agreement related to the fund. Cornyn said he isn't prepared to vote "yes" without an agreement.

The Senate Judiciary Committee was set to vote on advancing Blanche's nomination Thursday, but late Wednesday, announced it had delayed the hearing.

Now, Mr. Trump has suggested he's willing to wait out Cornyn and Tillis.

"Todd Blanche is a STAR, and everyone knows it!" the president posted on Truth Social. "He has the potential to go down as one of the Greatest Attorney Generals of All Time. However, John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting."

The president added. "I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd's name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office."

On Thursday, Cornyn said he received an updated offer from the Justice Department Wednesday night and sent back a counter proposal. But he said he's getting some pushback from "higher ups" at the White House. Cornyn said he wants Blanche to recommit to what he said in his testimony about the "anti-weaponization fund" being "dead," but claimed Blanche doesn't want to put it in writing.

"We want to make sure that it remains dead, and that the president isn't given any immunity from future audits that the ordinary taxpayer would not enjoy," he told CBS News on Thursday.

Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, speaks to reporters on Capitol Hill, Thursday, July 30, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein) Mark Schiefelbein

Tillis seemed more optimistic about a resolution, but said he believes someone at the White House is "giving the president bad advice."

"The only reason why we wouldn't move forward with this language is because that same adviser wants to bring it back to life at some point," he said.

Cornyn said he and Tillis aren't the only senators with concerns.

"POTUS is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis," Cornyn posted on X Thursday.

GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, another outgoing Republican, said "Todd Blanche cannot give commitments that Cornyn and Tillis want."

CBS News asked Cassidy whether he would support Blanche if the vote happened today.

"I'm not going to answer that because I'm still in the information gathering stage," Cassidy said.

If the president decides to pull and delay Blanche's nomination, it's not clear what the makeup of the Senate will be after the midterms. Tillis said the president's bet is a "gable."

"So I think, and you know, after the midterms, who knows who's going to be the next United States senator from North Carolina or Texas?" Tillis said.

World.title: Grants halted at agency devoted to safety of U.S. healthcare
World.content:
The Trump administration has effectively shut down most of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality's activities, closing the spigot on federal funding estimated to have saved thousands of lives and billions of dollars over the past 27 years by improving medical practice.

In a July 15 letter, the small Department of Health and Human Services agency known as AHRQ told researchers it was halting at least 104 grants, many aimed at improving patient safety. Although Congress appropriated $345 million for AHRQ for this fiscal year, the agency has spent less than $15 million on grants and hasn't issued a new one in over a year, according to a review of federal records. About 75% of agency staffers have been fired or quit since President Donald Trump took office last year, according to HHS.

Trump and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have sought to slash the federal government's investment in biomedical research, terminating grants and forcing scientists out of agencies across the health department. The gutting of AHRQ strikes some of the administration's critics as particularly shortsighted, though, because of the agency's noncontroversial focus on patient safety and its overall alignment with Trump and Kennedy's "Make American Healthy Again" campaign against chronic illness.

"When you think about everything Americans hate about our health care system — that it costs too much, that you can't get in to see a physician, that the treatment isn't right, that the records contain wrong information — all that is what AHRQ studies," said Aaron Carroll, chief executive of AcademyHealth, a health services research group that supports AHRQ's work.

The Trump and Kennedy changes to AHRQ appear intended to be permanent. All of AHRQ's grant managers have been fired, so there would be no way for AHRQ to directly oversee future grants, said Brent Sandmeyer, a former AHRQ program officer. "You wonder about this administration's commitment to fighting fraud," he said.

HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard said AHRQ intended to establish a new "framework" for grants. She did not reply to requests for further details.

Researchers who received the letter from AHRQ Director Roger Klein expressed bewilderment because much of their work has the same objectives that Klein highlighted as the agency's current priorities.

"AHRQ is the only federal agency that's focused on safety and quality," said Hardeep Singh, director of the Houston Methodist Safety, Quality and Well-Being Institute. His research, funded until recently by AHRQ, has aimed to reduce medical errors introduced by inadequate software design.

Klein stated that AHRQ's research interests include patient safety, preventing antibiotic resistance, countering overmedication of children, promotion of digital health tools, and research "focused on scientifically valid, measurable health outcomes and solution-oriented approaches in health disparities research."

KFF Health News examined about 20 of the canceled grants and found that nearly all had objectives that overlapped with the priorities Klein outlined.

"If there's an ideology, lay it out clearly. But there's no clarity whatsoever," said Goutham Rao, chairman of the Department of Family Medicine and Community Health at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland. AHRQ has funded Rao's work for 16 years and ended three of his department's current grants.

As an AHRQ-funded researcher since 2010, Rao has produced work that led to new approaches for common problems seen in doctors' offices, such as how to respond to weight loss in aged and frail patients. His work has helped reduce diagnostic tests in the elderly and improve hypertension screening of children.

"The priorities they lay out in that letter make me think they didn't even look at what we were doing," said Andrea Shields, a University of Connecticut OB-GYN whose AHRQ grant was also eliminated.

Shields developed and implemented training of nonspecialist doctors, nurses, and emergency medical technicians to deal with high-risk pregnancies. Women in rural areas are two to three times as likely to die during pregnancy as those elsewhere in the U.S.

A long legacy

AHRQ-funded research has been key to improving patient safety, structuring medical information technology, and introducing the concept of patient-centered care into the health system.

The agency is perhaps best known for its work on curbing hospital infections. Practices introduced because of AHRQ-funded studies prevented an estimated 20,500 deaths and saved $7.7 billion in healthcare costs from 2014 to 2017 alone, according to an analysis the agency conducted.

Teams at Harvard, Yale, and Rand in Santa Monica, California, developed a national standardized patient survey that HHS and healthcare systems use to refine healthcare practices with patient perspectives in mind, said Susan Edgman-Levitan, who has worked on that project since 1995 but recently lost her funding. She and her colleagues developed a definition of patient- and family-centered care that became a pillar of healthcare evaluation. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services bases some of its payments on hospital surveys her group designed.

AHRQ researchers working on five-year grants typically get letters confirming their award in the summer or fall each year. Last year, Edgman-Levitan said, they got no word and no money. They wrote a letter to Klein but heard "not a peep" in response. Then, around 5 p.m. on July 15, an emailed termination notice arrived. The $1 million annual grant was for developing hospital surveys regarding childbirth and behavioral health services.

"My salary is gone. The salaries of all my research assistants, survey scientists, all lost. It's terrible," she said. "But I'm near the end of my career. The salary piece is not as devastating as the loss of what I view as really critical work and support for improving childbirth care and patient care in general."

Klein, a molecular pathologist and Federalist Society-affiliated lawyer who took over the agency last July, has told staff that artificial intelligence can replace much of the evidence review and analytics done by AHRQ scientists, according to one current and one recently departed AHRQ official, whom KFF Health News agreed not to name to protect their jobs.

Such comments align with a report issued July 22 by White House science adviser Michael Kratsios, which said the government should "refocus support on individual scientists rather than legacy institutions, diversify funding mechanisms beyond slow consensus peer review," and build the future with AI.

Klein did not respond to requests for comment. HHS spokesperson Hilliard also did not respond to specific questions about AHRQ's plans or objectives.

Of the July 15 letter, Hilliard said: "Under statute, the AHRQ director must determine whether continuation funding is in the best interest of the federal government. AHRQ determined that certain non-competing continuation grants and jointly funded grants would not receive continuation awards."

Hilliard said the grants were not terminated but rather were "not awarded continued funding." This subtlety may have legal relevance for grantees planning to sue the administration, said Lauren Adams, a spokesperson for AcademyHealth.

"None of it makes any sense"

The Society for General Internal Medicine sued Klein and health secretary Kennedy last August over AHRQ's failure to issue new grants. The lawsuit, which is pending, argues that failure to use most of AHRQ's $369 million fiscal 2025 appropriation is illegal under a 1974 law intended to protect Congress' power of the purse.

"None of it makes any sense," said Nora Becker, an internist at Michigan Medicine who lost the last two years of a five-year training and research grant on the relationship between financial difficulty and health outcomes. "The MAHA agenda could fit nicely with AHRQ priorities — we focus on chronic conditions, the quality of care, deprescribing, identifying harms of overmedication."

She added: "To be honest, it doesn't feel like any of this is being done in good faith. Part of me just wonders whether the goal was to destroy AHRQ. But I don't know why AHRQ was such a target."

Hilliard said that "the Trump Administration remains committed to the responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars."

In March 2025, Kennedy announced plans to fold AHRQ and parts of other HHS agencies into a new Office of Strategy. But Congress has shown no interest in the reorganization plan.

Klein hasn't publicly commented about AHRQ's overall objectives or plans since attacking previous AHRQ activities in a Newsweek opinion piece he co-wrote with an assistant that was published in January.

The article argued that under previous administrations, "scientific neutrality" had given way to "moral signaling" on diversity and equity. But now, Klein wrote, the Trump administration had righted AHRQ's focus to "generate evidence that improves how health care is delivered."

Klein has held no agency-wide meetings, has declined to meet with AHRQ supporters and grantees, and never announced a blueprint for the agency, according to current and former AHRQ employees. They said he is infrequently seen at the agency's Rockville, Maryland, offices.

Staff members currently number 74, Hilliard said, down from about 300 in early 2025. The agency has halted about $100 million in this year's commitments to grantees, a substantial chunk of its congressionally approved budget, according to a tabulation by AcademyHealth.

"These claims about Dr. Klein are pointedly false," Hilliard said. "AHRQ is strengthening its grants process, reviewing agency work for quality, aligning with its statutory mission, and focusing on research to improve patient outcomes."

She did not respond to a request for specific information on grant funding.

AHRQ continues to conduct some data collection and has kept up its Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, which measures how Americans use and pay for medical care, insurance, and out-of-pocket costs. However, publication has slowed to a trickle because Klein reviews every piece of data or report issued by the agency, said Elisabeth Kato, who worked at AHRQ for 16 years before resigning from a senior position in April.

AHRQ also runs the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, a panel whose assessments on the value of drugs and procedures determine whether insurers are required to cover them.

The task force hasn't met since March 2025. Trump fired two of the group's senior leaders and currently has only six of the 16 members it had when he took office. "The longer they don't meet, the longer we're losing connection between evidence and coverage," said Sandmeyer, one of the former AHRQ officials.

A meeting of the task force is set for the end of August, Hilliard said.

Pediatrician Courtney Mangus lost her grant in the middle of a five-year project aimed at reducing cancers by using a software tool to help reduce the number of CT scans done on children who come to emergency rooms with abdominal pain. In rural and community emergency rooms, children are much more likely to be scanned for appendicitis than they are in better-equipped children's pediatric hospitals. Each scan contributes to cancer risk.

Mangus wonders how AHRQ's disappearance as a funding source will affect her career. "I need some funding to finish what I've started," she said, "so then I could apply for bigger awards that can move the needle on this issue."

She has applied to smaller foundations and may seek support from the National Institutes of Health, but her work was "really best suited for AHRQ."

As NIH, AHRQ, and other federal funders have cut grants over the past two years, new applications have flooded private biomedical foundations.

"It's baffling to me why AHRQ refuses to fund research that has legally been appropriated by Congress and signed by the president," Carroll said. "I don't understand why everyone else in government isn't going out of their mind about this."

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

Correction: This article was updated to reflect that the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force does not assess vaccines and to correct the type of medicine that Nora Becker practices.
