What’s On Tonight

Live Samba & MPB Night (programming confirmed day-of on Instagram Stories) — at Rio Scenarium, 21:00 – 03:00. Thursday kicks off the weekend with the city’s most celebrated live music house. Multiple acts across three floors set the standard for a classic Carioca night.

Street Bar & Boteco Crawl — at Avenida Mem de Sá / Arcos da Lapa, 21:00 – 02:00. The Thursday warm-up sees crowds spilling out of bars onto the pedestrian strip. The vibe is noisy, cheap, and unpretentious—perfect for a newcomer to feel the city’s pulse.

After-Work Cocktails & Dinner Scene — at Rua Dias Ferreira, Leblon, 20:00 – 01:00. Leblon’s glitziest strip comes alive, packed with professionals and expats. A strong Thursday date-night energy with some of the best mixology in Zona Sul.

Hipster Bar & Patio Night — at Rua Nelson Mandela / Cobal do Humaitá, Botafogo, 20:00 – 01:00. A younger, artsy crowd gathers on the lively streets of Botafogo for craft drafts and casual conversation, a perfect low-pressure entry into the city’s social scene.

Bossa Nova & Jazz Evenings — at Lounge Bars around Praça General Osório, Ipanema, 21:00 – 00:00. Subtle, sophisticated sounds fill the intimate bars of Ipanema. Go for a quieter, romantic alternative to the samba chaos of Lapa.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Warm-up (20:00-22:00): Start in Leblon or Ipanema for an upscale dinner and cocktails. Rua Dias Ferreira is where the well-heeled Carioca begins the night.

Pre-peak (22:00-00:00): Head to Botafogo’s Rua Nelson Mandela for a more casual, indie bar crawl with a younger crowd, or dive straight into the Lapa street bars under the arches.

Late-night peak (00:00-04:00): The serious samba and MPB fans pile into Rio Scenarium or the Lapa street party peaks until 3 am. This is where the night hits its sweaty, musical stride.

Sunrise (04:00+): The hardcore migrate to all-night botecos or post-club street food in Lapa. Grab a pastel and a final beer before Ubering home.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba & Pagode — The percussive heartbeat of Rio. Live drums, cavaquinho, and call-and-response singing in historic heritage buildings or boisterous backstreet bars. Where: Rio Scenarium, Bar do Omar, Beco do Rato (Lapa)

MPB & Bossa Nova — Smooth, poetic, and melodic Brazilian popular music. Intimate settings where the songwriting takes center stage. Where: Toca do Vinícius, Vinícius Show Bar (Ipanema)

Electronic & House — Deep house and techno in dark, industrial spaces or open-air parties, often with a sophisticated, international crowd. Where: D-Edge (occasional pop-ups in Rio), Fosfobox (Copacabana)

Forró — Accordion-driven northeastern dance music. Sweaty, close-hold partner dancing, extremely accessible for beginners. Where: Feira de São Cristóvão (weekends), some Lapa clubs

Funk Carioca — Rio’s raw, bass-heavy baile sound. 150 bpm beats, often in favela parties or specific Zona Norte clubs; approach with a trusted local. Where: Baile da Gaiola (complex access), specific Zona Norte venues

Sertanejo — Brazilian country-pop. Huge in mainstream clubs, with singalong anthems about love and heartbreak. Where: Various large halls in Barra da Tijuca

Pick Your Night

Date night: Rua Dias Ferreira in Leblon. The street is essentially one long, glamorous restaurant row. Book a table for two, people-watch, and enjoy top-tier cocktails.

Solo and safe: Rio Scenarium in Lapa. It’s structured, secure, has a cloakroom, and uses a comanda system. You can enjoy the music alone without feeling out of place, and the security guards are visible.

Dance till sunrise: The Lapa Arches street circuit. Start at the kiosks on Av. Mem de Sá, follow the live music spilling from bars, and end up in an all-night samba joint like Beco do Rato.

Meet locals: Botafogo’s Rua Nelson Mandela and Cobal do Humaitá. Patio tables are communal by necessity, the beer is craft, and the crowd is a friendly mix of students and artists.

Chill and conversation: A live bossa nova bar near Praça General Osório in Ipanema. Tables are small, the music is low enough to talk, and the ambiance is pure Zona Sul sophistication.

Where to Go

Rio Scenarium — Lapa Rio’s most famous nightlife institution. A three-story antique shop by day, transforming into a spectacular live samba and MPB venue by night. The dance floor is a mix of foreign visitors and middle-class Cariocas. Tonight: Thursday is traditionally the start of the busy weekend with live bands playing from 9:30 pm. Exact lineup is typically posted on Instagram Stories the day of. Best time: Thursday-Saturday; live music starts 9:30 pm, peak energy at midnight. Arrive by 9:15 pm to secure a table without a painful queue. Cost: Entry coupon typically R$50-80, usually including a first drink. Caipirinhas R$30-40. Card and cash accepted; comanda system used. Address: Rua do Lavradio, 20, Lapa, Centro Getting there: Metro to Carioca/Cinelândia then a short Uber, or direct rideshare from Zona Sul. Do not walk on dark side streets. Good to know: Highly recommended for groups; smart-casual dress is essential. No beach flip-flops or singlets.

Lapa Arches & Av. Mem de Sá Street Bars — Lapa The open-air engine room of Rio’s nightlife. A dense strip of botecos and live-music bars spilling onto the pedestrianized street under the iconic white arches. Tonight: Thursday is a lively warm-up for the weekend, with crowds, street vendors, and cheap drinks from 9 pm. It feels like one large, informal street party. Best time: Wednesday through Saturday. The street fills up by 11:30 pm and goes until 3 am. Arrive at 10 pm if you want a seat. Cost: Street caipirinhas R$15-25, bottled beer R$10-15. Some indoor bars have a small couvert artistico if a band is playing. Cash is faster at kiosks; bars take cards. Address: Avenida Mem de Sá and surrounding streets near Praça Cardeal Câmara, Lapa Getting there: Metro to Cinelândia, then a 10-minute walk up the main lit avenue, or take an Uber directly to the Arcos. Good to know: No booking needed; casual streetwear. Keep phone and wallet in front pockets.

Rua Dias Ferreira Strip — Leblon The Beverly Hills of Rio’s nightlife. A single street housing dozens of high-end wine bars, gastropubs, and innovative cocktail lounges. Tonight: A buzzing Thursday night scene for the local ‘after-work’ crowd. The street is packed with well-dressed patrons from 8 pm spilling out of venues. Best time: Tuesday to Saturday, 8 pm-1 am. The prime time for a table is 8:30 pm. Cost: Cocktails and imported wines R$35-55. Card widely preferred; 10% service added to bills. Address: Rua Dias Ferreira, Leblon Getting there: Metro to Antero de Quental (Line 4) and a short, very safe walk, or direct Uber. Good to know: Book a table for dinner to avoid disappointment; dress smart-casual, no beachwear.

Bar Urca & Mureta da Urca — Urca A classic, no-frills boteco famous for its caipirinhas and empadas. Locals sit on the seawall (‘mureta’) across the street, watching the boats and the Christ the Redeemer statue. Tonight: A sunset ritual rather than a late-night bash. Go before 8 pm to grab a spot on the wall. Best time: Any sunny day; sunset hours. Arrive by 5:30 pm-6:30 pm for the best wall seats. Cost: Caipirinhas R$25-30, empadas R$8-12. Cash and cards both fine. Address: Rua Cândido Gaffrée, 205, Urca Phone: +55 21 2295-8747 Instagram: @barurcaoficial Getting there: Not on the metro line; an easy Uber ride from Botafogo or Copacabana. Good to know: No bookings; a casual pre-drink stop. Arrive early, order at the counter, and cross the street to the wall.

Cobal do Humaitá — Botafogo/Humaitá A large, vibrant gourmet market square ringed by bars and restaurants with open-air communal seating. It feels like a food-truck park with fixed infrastructure. Tonight: Always busy on Thursdays with a young, post-work crowd; it’s the social hub of Botafogo’s creative class. Best time: Tuesday to Saturday, 7 pm-1 am. The sweet spot is 8:30 pm. Cost: Craft beer R$20-30, dishes R$40-70. Most vendors accept cards. Comanda system common. Address: Rua Voluntários da Pátria, 446 – Humaitá Instagram: @cobaldohumaita Getting there: A 10-minute walk from Botafogo metro station, or a quick Uber. Good to know: No booking needed for the common areas; find a free spot and order at the bar counters.

Fosfobox — Copacabana A subterranean ‘club-in-a-box’ with a grungy, indie feel. The soundtrack varies from rock and pop to deep house, attracting a cool, alternative crowd that rejects the mainstream beach vibe. Tonight: Check Instagram @fosfobox for tonight’s specific DJ or party theme. It usually runs Thursday-Saturday. Best time: Friday and Saturday are peak, but Thursday offers a more relaxed door policy. Doors open 11 pm, peak at 1:30 am. Arrive after midnight. Cost: Entry R$30-60 depending on the event. Drinks R$20-30. Card accepted. Address: Rua Siqueira Campos, 143, Copacabana Instagram: @fosfobox Getting there: Metro to Siqueira Campos station, then a 3-minute walk. Safe area on main streets. Good to know: No booking needed; casual alternative dress. Bouncers are strict about IDs.

Pavão Azul — Copacabana An unfussy, legendary cheap-chop bar (‘pé sujo’) famous for its icy draft beer, stuffed crab, and chaotic sidewalk seating. A true Carioca cultural experience. Tonight: Packed every Thursday with a noisy mix of locals, expats, and beachgoers who never left. Best time: Any night; get there by 8 pm to grab a plastic chair on the pavement. Cost: Chopp (draft beer) R$10-12, portions R$40-60. Cash preferred, though cards are likely accepted. Address: Rua Hilário de Gouveia, 71, Copacabana Phone: +55 21 2236-2381 Getting there: A 5-minute walk from Cardeal Arcoverde metro. Streets are busy, but avoid the beach side at night. Good to know: Impossible to book; squeeze in where you can. Don’t be precious about personal space.

Leviano Bar — Lapa A cornerstone of Lapa’s club-bar hybrid scene, serving food and drinks upstairs, with a sweaty, raucous dance floor downstairs featuring samba, samba-rock, and MPB. Tonight: Thursday has a solid local turnout for the live band and DJ sets that mix classic samba with soul and funk. Best time: Thursday through Saturday, 10 pm-3 am. The band usually starts around 11:30 pm. Cost: Entry R$20-40; caipirinhas R$20-30. Address: Mem de Sá, 47, Lapa Instagram: @levianobar Getting there: Directly on Av. Mem de Sá under the arches. Easy access from the street party. Good to know: No booking needed; come as you are, but avoid beach flip-flops.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Lapa: The bohemian, chaotic cradle of samba. A loud, dense, and intoxicating clash of tourists, students, and street-party veterans.

Leblon: Affluent, polished, and airy. Where wealthy Cariocas and expats go for long dinners that turn into cocktail crawls on a single, chic street.

Ipanema: Sophisticated and balanced, mixing beach-life ease with serious bars, jazz clubs, and a strong LGBTQ+ presence.

Botafogo: Young, indie, and creative. The epicentre of Rio’s craft-beer and casual-patio movement, buzzing with students and young professionals.

Copacabana: A nostalgic, demographically mixed blend of old-school botecos, tourist traps, and hidden indie clubs, all set against a dramatic crescent beach.

Urca: Sleepy, safe, and scenic. A timeless village neighbourhood where the nightlife is literally sitting on a wall with a cold drink.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Teatro Odisséia (Lapa) — A three-floor club in a historic building with diverse music and a very inclusive, mixed crowd. The Thursday night scene draws a queer and alternative audience that bridges music genres.

Rua Farme de Amoedo (Ipanema) — Known colloquially as Rio’s gay street. The bars and beach kiosks near this strip are heavily frequented by the LGBTQ+ community and are safe, welcoming, and lively, especially on a Thursday evening.

Money & How Paying Works The Comanda Card: At almost every club and large bar, you swap your ID for a paper card upon entry. Every single drink or food item is marked on it. You pay the total at the exit cashier. Losing this card incurs a heavy penalty, often a flat fee of R$200-300, so guard it like your passport. Live Music Cover (Couvert Artístico): If there is a band playing, expect an automatic charge of R$30-80 per person added to your bill, regardless of whether you asked for it. It is standard and unavoidable. Card vs. Cash: Zona Sul’s major venues all take credit and debit cards, including contactless. For the Lapa street bars and kiosks, carry R$100-150 in cash for speed. Tipping: The standard ‘serviço’ is 10%, almost always included in your final bill total. You do not need to add extra tip unless the service was truly outstanding.

Getting Home Safe

Metro closes at midnight exactly (Monday-Saturday). If you plan to use the metro home, you must leave the venue by 11:30 pm to walk to the station safely.

99 and Uber are your lifelines after midnight. Wait for your ride inside the venue or the building lobby; never wait on a dark, empty street staring at your phone screen.

At 3 am in Lapa, surge pricing can be brutal. Walk up to one of the official yellow taxis parked near the main Police Post on the square under the Lapa Arches to negotiate a fixed fare or insist on the meter on night tariff ‘bandeira 2’.

Stay on the main lit strips. In Lapa, this means Av. Mem de Sá and the immediate Arches area. Avoid the cobblestone backstreets and empty squares. In Copacabana, use the Avenida Atlântica or Nossa Senhora de Copacabana, never the beach sand.

Adopt the ‘burner’ or secondary phone strategy. Keep your main smartphone hidden in your front trouser pocket or a cross-body bag. Use a cheap older phone for checking maps and Uber if you need to do so on the street.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time should I really arrive? If a venue says ‘starts 10 pm’, isn’t 10:15 pm fine?

For Lapa samba clubs, arriving at 10 pm gets you the last available table. For Botafogo bars, 8 pm is empty, 9 pm is buzzing. For a street party, showing up before midnight is an early warm-up; the real mess starts around 1 am.

Can I wear shorts and flip-flops to the club?

No. Even in Rio’s heat, nightlife dress codes, especially at samba houses like Rio Scenarium or Leblon bars, explicitly or socially reject beach flip-flops and singlets. Jeans, a t-shirt, and trainers or casual shoes are the universal safe uniform.

Is my English going to be a problem?

At the tourist-famous spots and high-end cocktail bars, staff often speak some English. At the gritty street botecos in Lapa or Pavão Azul, almost nobody will. Having a few key Portuguese phrases (‘Dois chopps, por favor’ – ‘Two draft beers, please’) will transform your night.

Sources: metrolinehub.com, rio.com, planrio.com

World.title: Guanacaste Airport Opens Premium PURA Lounge at Liberia
World.content:
The next time you fly out of Liberia, you now have somewhere to wait that isn’t a gate seat. Guanacaste Airport has opened PURA Lounge, a 354-square-meter (3,810-square-foot) premium waiting area on the departures level facing Gate 8, with windows looking out over the apron.

Check your departure time before you plan around it. The lounge runs daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., which covers the morning and midday departure bank when most flights to the United States and Canada leave. If your flight goes out in the evening, you will clear security to a closed door.

Getting in works three ways. Priority Pass and LoungeKey members are covered by their existing memberships. Everyone else can buy a day pass on the spot, no airline or cabin class required. The airport has not published a rate for the day pass, so you will find out the price at the counter.

Inside there are cushioned seating areas, semi-private zones if you want to shut out the terminal, and showers, which is the amenity that matters most here. Liberia sits in the dry Pacific northwest, and passengers routinely arrive at the airport straight off a beach or a long drive from Nosara, Santa Teresa or the Papagayo resorts with no chance to clean up. High-speed Wi-Fi, charging points, televisions and planted green areas fill out the rest of the space.

Food service covers breakfast and lunch depending on when you arrive, with a self-service station for coffee, soft drinks and Costa Rican liquors. The airport operates the lounge directly rather than contracting it out, which means complaints and requests go to airport staff instead of a third-party concessionaire.

The interior design follows what the airport calls a sense-of-place concept, drawing on the plains, mountains, forests and beaches of Guanacaste. The lounge logo is built from the seed pod of the guanacaste tree, the national tree that gives the province its name.

The build represents a $1.4 million investment by Coriport, the concessionaire that holds the operating rights to Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport under the VINCI Airports network. The lounge created seven direct jobs in customer service, catering and cleaning, and every position went to a Guanacaste resident.

“PURA Lounge reinforces Guanacaste Airport’s position as a modern terminal committed to delivering a high-quality travel experience,” said Renata González, commercial and communications manager at Guanacaste Airport. “We want every passenger to find a space that combines comfort, hospitality and the Pura Vida spirit that defines our region.”

The opening lands in the middle of a wider build-out at Costa Rica’s second-busiest international airport. Liberia has absorbed steady passenger growth as airlines add North American and European routes, and a separate private-aviation terminal financed by Signature Aviation is planned for the same site. Airport management has tied both projects to the same argument, that better facilities at Liberia keep high-spending visitors flying directly into Guanacaste rather than routing through San José and driving four hours west.

Liberia’s terminal has limited seating and limited food options once you are past security, and departure days in Guanacaste often start early. Eight hours a day so there is now an alternative.

World.title: Costa Rica Wins Its First Surfing Gold Medal in Regional Games History
World.content:
Costa Rican surfer Rachel Agüero Cabezas won the women’s shortboard title at the Central American and Caribbean Games in the Dominican Republic tpday, delivering Costa Rica its first gold medal in surfing in the history of the regional competition.

The 20-year-old beat Barbados’ Chelsea Tuach 10.50 points to 7.33 in the final at Playa Encuentro in Cabarete, on the northern coast of Puerto Plata province. Agüero’s score came from two waves graded 5.83 and 4.67, while Tuach posted a 5.00 and a 2.33. According to the National Olympic Committee, Agüero took control of the heat from the opening minutes and never surrendered the lead. Tuach needed a wave scored at 5.51 or better to overturn the result and never found one.

Agüero reached the final by eliminating the surfer most observers had installed as the favorite. In the fourth round she defeated Nicaragua’s Candelaria Resano, an Olympian and world championship medalist, by 12.57 points to 11.33. She had opened the competition on the first day of the event with 11.16 points, built on waves of 7.33 and 3.83, to win her heat ahead of Puerto Rico’s Havanna Cabrero and Colombia’s Margarita Conde. That 7.33 stood as the highest-scoring women’s wave of the opening day.

The result caps a season that has established Agüero as the leading woman in Costa Rican competitive surfing. She arrived in the Dominican Republic as the two-time national Open champion, having sealed her second consecutive title only weeks earlier at the closing round of the Banco LAFISE national circuit at Playa Hermosa de Jacó, the beach where she lives and trains.

In March she won the Denga Santa Teresa Pro at Playa Carmen. She has also been competing on World Surf League regional events, the tier where surfers accumulate the results and ranking points that open the door to the sport’s professional circuits. Costa Rica had never won a surfing gold medal at these Games before Wednesday. The country’s only previous podium finishes in the sport came at San Salvador 2023, when Lía Díaz and Anthony Flores each took bronze in longboard.

Sam Reidy added another on Tuesday, beating the Dominican Republic’s Gian Marco Oliva 14.50 to 11.60 in the men’s shortboard bronze heat, a result the Costa Rican Surf Federation described as the first shortboard medal at the Games. Flores finished fourth in the men’s longboard event this year after losing his bronze heat to Mexico’s Heriberto Torres.

The surfing competition ran from July 25 until today at Playa Encuentro, a break that has become one of the Caribbean’s most reliable competitive venues, and drew 71 surfers from 12 countries across shortboard, longboard and stand-up paddle surf. Agüero’s medal was Costa Rica’s third gold of Santo Domingo 2026. The first two came in taekwondo, through Jaycee Bassett and Neshy Lindo.

This edition of the Games is the 25th and marks a century since the first was held in Mexico City in 1926. Organizers programmed 40 sports, more than the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic schedule, and more than 6,200 athletes from 37 countries and territories are competing over 16 days.

Costa Rican surfing has been producing this kind of result with increasing regularity. Díaz became the first surfer from Costa Rica or anywhere in Central America to qualify for the World Surf League’s Longboard Tour, a circuit that opened its season at Huntington Beach in California this month.

Leilani McGonagle won a place on the 2026-27 Challenger Series, the qualifying tier immediately below the elite Championship Tour. Bodyboarder Dulce Agüero reached a podium at Pipeline in Hawaii in March. The national federation has said its planning is now oriented around the qualifying events for the 2028 Olympics, where surfing will again be on the program.

For Agüero, the initial reward is a regional title at 20 and a clear line of sight to the next stage. The Pan American Games in Lima in 2027 come first, and the Olympic qualifying calendar follows behind it.

World.title: Costa Rica Moves to Treat Illegal Mining as Organized Crime
World.content:
Costa Rican lawmakers have given initial approval to legislation that would allow authorities to pursue illegal mining and other serious environmental offenses using organized-crime laws. The Legislative Assembly approved the proposal in first debate with 53 votes.

All five political groups represented in Congress supported the measure, reflecting growing concern about criminal networks involved in illegal gold extraction, logging and wildlife trafficking. The bill would apply when environmental crimes are carried out by a structured group of at least two people working together.

That change could give prosecutors access to investigative tools normally reserved for organized-crime cases, including intercepted communications, longer investigative periods and extended pretrial detention. Supporters argue that the current system is better suited to prosecuting individuals caught carrying out an illegal activity than identifying the financiers, organizers and logistics networks behind it.

The problem has become particularly visible in Crucitas, a rural area near the Nicaraguan border where illegal gold mining has continued for years. Authorities have repeatedly found organized operations involving machinery, transportation, fuel, processing equipment and the illegal sale of gold.

The proposal would increase penalties when mining offenses are linked to a coordinated criminal group. Mining exploration or extraction inside national parks, biological reserves, wildlife refuges and other protected state land would carry sentences ranging from three months to five years. When the crime is committed by an organized group, the penalty could rise to between three and six years in prison.

The changes would also cover illegal logging, wildlife trafficking, fishing offenses and crimes involving sea turtles. For some offenses under Costa Rica’s wildlife, forestry, fisheries and marine turtle laws, organized-crime involvement could add between two and four years to the existing prison sentence.

The reform would also eliminate situations in which defendants accused of serious environmental crimes can avoid prison by paying only a fine. Lawmakers backing the measure said many existing penalties are so low that prosecutors cannot use the investigative powers needed to dismantle larger networks.

The legislation is intended to distinguish between someone acting alone and a structured group that recruits workers, supplies equipment, transports illegally obtained material and collects the profits. The proposal does not authorize gold mining in Crucitas.

A separate bill would allow regulated gold exploration and mining in the Cutris district of San Carlos. That proposal remains under discussion in the Legislative Assembly’s Environment Committee. The distinction is important because debate over the future of Crucitas has divided Costa Rican political parties and environmental groups.

Some lawmakers and government officials argue that regulated mining would allow the state to regain control of the area and collect revenue from its gold deposits. Opponents say reopening large-scale mining could cause further environmental damage and reward the failure to stop illegal extraction.

The organized-crime proposal has attracted broader political support because it addresses illegal activity without changing Costa Rica’s general prohibition on open-pit metal mining. The bill still faces additional legislative steps before becoming law.

A second debate was scheduled for tomorrow. However, lawmakers are expected to return the proposal to an earlier point so they can make changes agreed upon by the political parties before holding another final vote. If eventually approved and signed, the reform would strengthen penalties in future cases where prosecutors can prove that environmental crimes were committed through an organized structure.

World.title: Costa Rica Warns of Poor Air Quality as Saharan Dust Arrives
World.content:
A new push of Saharan dust is expected to spread across Costa Rica this week, bringing hazy skies, reduced visibility and poorer air quality, with Thursday and Friday forecast to be the most difficult days. The dust will affect nearly all of Costa Rica, although higher concentrations are expected in Alajuela, western parts of the Central Valley and some areas of Cartago.

Residents may notice a pale or milky appearance in the sky known as calima, caused by fine particles suspended in the atmosphere. Visibility over mountains and other distant landmarks could also become noticeably worse. The conditions are expected to become more apparent beginning Wednesday before reaching their strongest point on Thursday, July 30, and Friday, July 31. Air quality should begin improving Saturday as the dust moves north toward other parts of Central America and Mexico.

People with asthma, allergies and other respiratory conditions face the greatest risk. Children and older adults should also reduce the amount of time they spend outdoors during the highest concentrations. The warning extends beyond people with existing health problems. Residents in generally good health are being advised to avoid long periods of strenuous outdoor activity on Thursday and Friday, including extended runs, cycling or outdoor exercise lasting several hours.

Fine particles carried within the dust can enter the respiratory system and cause irritation. Possible symptoms include coughing, itchy eyes or throat, headaches, chest discomfort, breathing difficulty and worsening asthma or allergy attacks. People who must remain outdoors should limit their exposure and consider wearing a well-fitting mask, particularly if they have respiratory problems. Anyone who develops discomfort while exercising should stop the activity and move indoors.

The Saharan dust originated over North Africa and traveled thousands of kilometers across the Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea before reaching Central America. These events are common during the middle of the year, when strong trade winds carry dry air and mineral particles westward.

The approaching dust will combine with stronger winds, locally raised soil particles, pollen and smoke still present from regional burning. Together, those elements can increase the amount of material suspended in the air even when the Saharan particles are not clearly visible. Lower rainfall will make the situation more noticeable. Rain normally helps remove dust and other particles from the atmosphere, but Costa Rica is expecting a significant reduction in precipitation over the next several days.

The dry air associated with Saharan dust can also limit the development of rain clouds, allowing particles to remain suspended longer. The episode is not expected to produce dangerously polluted conditions across the country. However, prolonged exposure could cause problems for sensitive people and make outdoor activity uncomfortable even for otherwise healthy residents.

You may also encounter hazier views from mountain overlooks, volcanoes and higher-elevation destinations. Flights are not currently expected to face major disruptions, although distant visibility could be reduced. Conditions are forecast to improve considerably over the weekend as the main concentration of dust moves away from Costa Rica.

World.title: Costa Rica Expels Second-Division Club for 10 Years Over Match-Fixing
World.content:
The Costa Rican Football Federation has thrown a second-division club out of the sport for ten years after its investigators concluded the team took part in manipulating four matches during the 2025 season, in what is now the fifth match-fixing case in Costa Rican football to end in sanctions.

The Disciplinary Commission of the Federación Costarricense de Fútbol found that Municipal Garabito Fútbol Club SAD, which competed in the Liga de Ascenso under the name San Carlos FC, breached Article 66 of the federation’s Disciplinary Code. The resolution bars the club from any football-related activity for a decade. The federation’s legal department has since notified every affiliated league — the first division, the Liga de Ascenso, the amateur Linafa structure, futsal, beach football and women’s football — that the prohibition applies to the legal entity regardless of category or format.

The case rests on a report by the federation’s Integrity Office, led by Carlos Ricardo Benavides, which examined four Liga de Ascenso fixtures from the 2024-2025 season. All four ended in lopsided defeats. San Carlos FC lost 8-2 to Quepos Cambute on January 19, 2025, fell 5-1 to Cofutpa on February 9, lost 6-2 away to Municipal Grecia on March 1, and lost 5-2 to Jicaral on March 9. According to the resolution, the investigation found a sustained pattern of irregularities in sports betting linked to matches the club played, together with atypical movement in betting markets.

Much of that evidence came from outside Costa Rica. Sportradar, the sports data firm that assists FIFA with integrity investigations, issued alerts on several of the club’s fixtures after analysing both the state of betting markets before kickoff and the swings recorded while games were in progress. In the Quepos Cambute match, San Carlos FC was leading 1-0 at the 27th minute when heavy money began moving on a San Carlos defeat; the game finished 8-2 to Quepos Cambute.

Sportradar filed a report flagging irregular movement five days later, on January 24. Investigators also drew on reports from the bookmakers Betway, VBet and 9 Olybet and from the International Betting Integrity Association. The Integrity Office concluded that the relationship between the market swings and what happened on the pitch pointed to a high probability of deliberate intervention by the club.

The commission’s finding, as set out in the resolution, is that Municipal Garabito Fútbol Club SAD, known as San Carlos FC, played an active part in the conduct. The franchise had been based in the Pacific canton of Garabito before its owners moved the operation north; the club then competed as San Carlos FC in the Northern Zone. It was relegated from the Liga de Ascenso at the end of the 2024-2025 season and did not subsequently compete in Linafa. The club has no connection to AD San Carlos of the first division, nor to Inter San Carlos, which recently won the Liga de Ascenso title.

Three players who turned out for the club were sanctioned in a separate resolution that became final on June 25 of this year. That file concerned an approach made in April 2025 to players at Deportivo Upala, who were offered money to lose a Liga de Ascenso fixture against San Carlos FC.

The attempt failed because the Upala players reported it. Hansell Arauz Ovares, a retired forward who won four national titles with Deportivo Saprissa between 2014 and 2016, and Henry Cooper Bennett, a former Limón FC striker, were each banned for 15 years. Goalkeeper Fabián Rodríguez Esquivel received 15 years in the same file and a further 20 years in a separate case in which the Integrity Office concluded he had approached a Guadalupe FC player about fixing a first-division match, bringing his total ban to 35 years. All three bans cover any football-related role, whether as a player, coaching staff or club official.

The club expulsion is the second of its kind in Costa Rica. Puerto Golfito FC was excluded for ten years in 2024 on similar grounds. In 2025, three Municipal Turrialba officials — Enrique Valencia, Ernesto de la Torre and Rolando Pereira — were suspended for five years over an alleged manipulation attempt. Each of the cases sanctioned so far has originated in the lower tiers of the Costa Rican game, where budgets are thin, wages are low and matches still attract enough betting volume abroad to make manipulation worth someone’s while.

In notifying every affiliated league of the expulsion, the federation asked each to apply its integrity protocols and strengthen preventive measures. The Integrity Office has indicated that further resolutions are pending.

World.title: Ride-app protest could slow your drive across the Valle Central this morning
World.content:
If you have a flight out of Juan Santamaría today, a shuttle booked to the airport, or a drive between Cartago and San José, leave earlier than you planned. Ride-app drivers have called a protest for 9 a.m. today, and the roads they say they will use are the ones that carry nearly everyone.

Organizers say the convoy will roll along Ruta 1 in Alajuela, through Ochomogo, past Sabanilla and onto Circunvalación, finishing at Casa Presidencial in Zapote. Those details come from the drivers themselves. As of first light Wednesday, the Policía de Tránsito had not published an advisory confirming the route, so treat that list as the plan rather than the result. Plans like this one shift, shrink or start late.

What the drivers have called is a tortuguismo, a go-slow. Nobody blocks anything. The convoy simply travels in a pack at a crawl, and every vehicle behind it travels at the same speed. That distinction is the whole story for you. A closure gets you a detour, an officer waving you around, and a police post you can see from a distance. A go-slow gets you none of that. There is no sign, no announcement, and no way to tell you are in it until you already are. Once you are boxed in on a divided highway, your only real option is to wait.

Ruta 1 is the reason this matters to travelers. It is the corridor between San José and Juan Santamaría, so anything that slows it slows every airport transfer, every hotel shuttle and every rental car heading for a return desk. Ochomogo sits on the climb between Cartago and San José and is the pinch point for that whole side of the valley. Circunvalación is the ring road that absorbs traffic coming off Ruta 27 and feeds it around the capital toward Zapote. Between them, those three points decide whether the Valle Central moves.

If you are flying out this morning and have not left yet, go now. Whatever cushion you would normally give yourself, add an hour on top of it. That sounds excessive on a normal Wednesday, and on a normal Wednesday it would be. The problem with a go-slow is that the delay is not proportional to the protest.

A few dozen vehicles moving at 20 kilometers per hour (about 12 miles per hour) for half an hour can leave a line that takes two hours to drain, because the road behind them keeps filling at normal speed while the front of it empties at a crawl. You do not lose the time the protest lasts. You lose the time it takes the backlog to clear.

Check in online before you leave, and if you have a bag to drop, know your airline’s cutoff rather than guessing at it. If you are running late, call the airline from the road rather than waiting until you reach the counter. Missing a bag cutoff by ten minutes is a different problem than missing a flight, and airlines can sometimes do something about the first if they hear from you early.

If you are already on Ruta 1 and traffic ahead of you dies, stay in the lane you are in. Weaving between lanes to get past a convoy does not work, and on that stretch it puts you alongside heavy trucks that cannot stop quickly. Do not try to overtake the group. If you have not yet committed to the highway, Ruta 3, the old road through Heredia and Alajuela, runs roughly parallel and gives you a way to reach the airport without joining the line. It is slower on a good day and it will be crowded today, but a slow road that is moving beats a fast road that is not.

Coming from Cartago, the alternative to Florencio del Castillo is the old road, and this week that carries a complication of its own. The Romería is already underway. Tránsito started its operation on July 25 with about 150 officers on that corridor and reinforces it between July 31 and August 2, and pilgrims are walking the shoulder in numbers. The old road is an option this morning, but drive it expecting people on foot rather than a clear run.

If you are not traveling and have nothing that cannot move, the simplest answer is to not drive between roughly 9 a.m. and midday. Reschedule the Zapote appointment. Take the errand in the afternoon. Every vehicle that stays home is one that is not in the line in front of somebody trying to catch a plane.

Behind all of this is a bill that has been moving through the Legislative Assembly for years. Expediente 23.736 would regulate transport offered through platforms such as Uber and DiDi, requiring drivers to register with the CCSS and Hacienda, pay an annual permit, and meet insurance and background requirements. The Comisión de Gobierno y Administración finished working through 282 mociones de fondo on Tuesday and approved nine of them, sending the revised text back to the plenary. That vote is what put drivers on the road this morning.

The drivers want two things added before it passes. They want a ceiling on the commission platforms take from each fare, and they want guaranteed benefits and due process when a company deactivates an account. Drivers made both demands at the Assembly earlier this month, saying they had not been heard during the drafting.

Aprimotec, an association representing platform drivers, asked the Assembly and the Executive on July 20 to stop the bill’s advance altogether, arguing the text was written around the traditional taxi sector and would push drivers out of the work rather than formalize it. The taxi sector sees it differently. Canatrans, Fenacotaxi, the Foro Nacional de Taxistas and other transport groups have publicly backed the bill, framing it as legal certainty and fair competition.

Neither side is likely to settle it this morning. What will be settled by lunchtime is whether you made your flight.

World.title: Five Belizean high-school girls turn a coastal crisis into an agricultural opportunity and win STEAM Award
World.content:
Five Belizean high-school girls turn a coastal crisis into an agricultural opportunity and win STEAM Award

By Ingrid Ferlo: What began as reluctant attendance at a STEAM Summer Camp culminated in national recognition for five students from Bishop Martin High School, whose proposal to transform sargassum seaweed into agricultural fertilizer earned the “Best Use of STEAM” Award at the 2026 STEAM Festival.

The winners, Linda Escalante, Ideleen Monzon, Vivian Martinez, Yasmin Minjangos and Marceline Locario, admit they almost never participated. Summer classes had already filled their mornings, while the STEAM camp occupied their afternoons. Some wanted to rest; others simply lacked enthusiasm. Encouragement from their mothers ultimately persuaded them to attend, a decision that would reshape their outlook.

Their interest in science and engineering developed through exposure to practical challenges rather than abstract theory. Teacher Wilson Mendoza challenged students to think about real environmental problems facing Belize. Industry professionals from ASR reinforced the idea that engineering is fundamentally about improving people’s lives. A visit to Orange Walk ITVET, where students observed AutoCAD being applied to real projects, demonstrated how mathematics underpins modern design and construction.

The result was “The Reborn of Sargassum”, a concept designed to address one of Belize’s most persistent environmental challenges. Rather than treating sargassum as waste, the students envisioned a boat capable of collecting the seaweed, compressing it, and processing it into fertilizer for Orange Walk’s agricultural sector. Their research suggested that sargassum contains nutrients that could benefit crops while helping combat fungal diseases, creating the prospect of cleaner beaches alongside healthier sugar cane production.

The proposal resonated because it connected environmental protection with economic development. The students believed their design could reduce the odour and disruption caused by decomposing sargassum along Belize’s coastline while creating value from material that is otherwise discarded. Community members, they said, recognized the potential benefits for businesses, restaurants and farmers alike.

Success, however, was far from assured. The team divided responsibilities according to individual strengths, assigning research, model construction and presentation tasks accordingly.

Faced with strong competition and rigorous questioning from judges, they feared they had fallen short. Their preparation proved decisive, particularly when judges questioned the chemical treatment of sargassum, an issue the students had researched by examining approaches used in Mexico.

The announcement of their victory came unexpectedly. Two team members had stepped away briefly when they heard their names called. The celebration that followed reflected not only relief but also a growing confidence that young women belong in science, technology, engineering, the arts and mathematics as much as anyone else.

Winning the award has not diminished their ambitions. The students now hope to develop a working prototype, but acknowledge that financing remains the principal obstacle. With support from organizations such as the sugar industry, the Inter-American Development Bank or other potential investors, who share their belief that innovative ideas deserve an opportunity to move beyond the classroom, they believe they could bring their prototype to life.

Their advice to other girls is simple: embrace opportunities that initially seem uncomfortable. A summer programme they almost declined has become the foundation for a project with the potential to tackle one of Belize’s most visible environmental challenges while supporting one of its most important industries.

World.title: Confidence down, imports up, exports down: what the new numbers mean for your wallet
World.content:
Confidence down, imports up, exports down: what the new numbers mean for your wallet

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Two reports landed from the Statistical Institute of Belize this week, and read together they explain a feeling many households already know without any survey: money is tight, and it is not your imagination.

Start with the mood. Consumer confidence measured 41.1 in June on a scale where anything under 50 means pessimism. Belizeans are especially wary of big purchases right now, with sentiment on buying appliances, furniture and vehicles falling hardest, down 8.5 percent in a single month. When families postpone the new fridge and patch up the old washing machine instead, that is what this number looks like in real life.

Now the trade report, which helps explain the mood. Belize imported $275.8 million worth of goods in June, up a hefty 21.3 percent from last year, and the increases came in exactly the categories that hit home: fuel, up $15.2 million partly on higher world prices, food up $12.1 million, and fertilizer costing farmers more. When the country pays more for fuel and food, so does every household at the pump and the shop counter.

Meanwhile the money flowing the other way shrank. Exports fell to $26.0 million for the month, with citrus struggling, sugar down and no formal cattle sales at all. For the half year, imports hit $1.65 billion against just $166.6 million in exports.

There is genuine hope in the data. Belizeans’ expectations for the next twelve months actually turned optimistic, crossing above 50 for the first time in months, and molasses, lobster and shrimp are earning more abroad.

So the honest summary: today feels hard, people believe better is coming, and the trade numbers say the squeeze is real. Do the numbers match what your household is living? Tell us in the comments.

World.title: Special Envoy calls for greater awareness to combat Human Trafficking
World.content:
Special Envoy calls for greater awareness to combat Human Trafficking

By Zoila Palma: Today is observed around the globe as World Day Against Trafficking in Persons.

Data from the United Nations indicate that about 70% of those investigated, prosecuted and convicted for trafficking in 2022 were men.

In addition, data shows that 74% of traffickers operate within organized crime groups.

Special Envoy for the Development of Families and Children Rosanna Briceno said that the theme “Trapped Behind the Scam” serves to shine a light on the growing threat of human trafficking hidden behind deceptive job offers, online scams, and false promises of a better life.

“Traffickers prey on vulnerability, using manipulation and fraud to lure victims into situations of exploitation from which escape can be difficult and dangerous. This year’s theme reminds us that human trafficking can happen to anyone, anywhere, and that awareness is one of our strongest tools for prevention,” the Special Envoy said.

The Special Envoy said that by learning to recognize the warning signs, promoting safe online practices, and supporting survivors, we can help protect individuals and communities from falling victim to these crimes.

World.title: Ministry of Health and Wellness launches Belize MOVES: A National Movement for Healthier Living
World.content:
Ministry of Health and Wellness launches Belize MOVES: A National Movement for Healthier Living

The Ministry of Health and Wellness (MOHW), in collaboration with the Caribbean Public Health Agency (CARPHA), under the CARICOM SPAIN project, “Strengthening Regional Leadership, Governance, and Coordinated Action in Health to Address New and Existing Health Challenges in the Caribbean Community (CARICOM),” and with support from the Taiwan International Cooperation and Development Fund (Taiwan ICDF), officially launched Belize MOVES, a national initiative aimed at inspiring Belizeans to embrace healthier lifestyles through increased physical activity, healthy nutrition, and regular health screenings.

Belize MOVES is Belize’s adaptation of the regional Caribbean MOVES initiative. It represents a significant milestone in the country’s efforts to prevent and reduce non-communicable diseases (NCDs), which account for approximately 65 percent of all deaths in Belize. Building on the success of the Love Your Heart initiative, Belize MOVES will expand evidence-based community wellness interventions into a sustainable national movement.

The initiative is founded on three strategic pillars: physical activity, healthy nutrition, and health screenings. It seeks to engage individuals, families, schools, workplaces, communities, and organizations in creating a culture where healthy choices become part of everyday life.

Speaking at the launch, Hon. Kevin Bernard, Minister of Health and Wellness, emphasized the importance of prevention and collective action. “Today, we are not simply launching another health program; we are launching a national movement. Belize MOVES is a promise that together we will build a healthier Belize through prevention, partnership, and community action.”

The Minister further reaffirmed the Government of Belize’s commitment to tackling the growing burden of NCDs through investments in prevention, primary health care, healthier schools, healthier workplaces, and healthier communities.

Speaking on behalf of the regional public health agency, CARPHA, Dr. Heather Armstrong, Head, Chronic Disease and Injury, welcomed the launch: “CARPHA is fully committed to helping Belize and all Member States promote healthier lifestyles, build stronger health systems, and create communities where healthy choices are easy to make. We are happy to stand with Belize today and be part of this launch—we hope this is the first of many moments, memories, and healthier lives.”

The official launch, which was held on July 23, 2026, at the Sir George Brown Park, featured cultural performances, community fitness demonstrations, health screenings, nutrition education, wellness exhibits, and family-friendly activities.

Belize MOVES will continue to roll out through community events, workplace wellness programs, school-based initiatives, public awareness campaigns, and strategic partnerships, beginning in Belmopan and Orange Walk before expanding nationwide.

The Ministry of Health and Wellness extends sincere appreciation to CARPHA, Taiwan ICDF, Pan American Health Organization/World Health Organization (PAHO/WHO), municipalities, community organizations, private-sector partners, health professionals, community health workers, and all stakeholders.

Together, Belize MOVES represents a bold step towards healthier communities, stronger prevention efforts, and improved quality of life for all Belizeans.

The Ministry invites every Belizean to move more, eat well, know your numbers, and encourage others to do the same.

Move Yuh Body! Move Belize!

World.title: Belizean hospitality workers soon to benefit from new group life and medical insurance partnership between Hotel Association and Sagicor
World.content:
Belizean hospitality workers soon to benefit from new group life and medical insurance partnership between Hotel Association and Sagicor

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belizean hospitality workers and their families are expected to benefit from a new group life and medical insurance plan launched through a partnership between the Belize Hotel Association and Sagicor.

The BHA Group Life and Medical Plan will allow eligible association member businesses to access corporate-grade insurance coverage at exclusive rates. The initiative is only the second of its kind in Belize and is intended to help employers strengthen their benefits packages while supporting the well-being and financial security of workers and their families.

Coverage options include health insurance, life insurance and accidental death and dismemberment benefits, with several price points available. The plan is open to BHA member businesses of varying sizes, and no underwriting is currently required to determine employee eligibility.

BHA President Reynaldo Malik said the partnership reflects the association’s commitment to providing meaningful value to its members and making important coverage more affordable and accessible.

Sagicor Senior Sales Associate Stephen Bermudez said the initiative would support employers and employees while helping to create a healthier and more secure hospitality workforce.

BHA members interested in eligibility, rates and enrolment information may contact the association’s Membership and Services Coordinator, Shamarie Lamb, or Sagicor.

World.title: Belize Forest Department and Belize Coast Guard plant more than 250 red mangrove propagules
World.content:
Belize Forest Department and Belize Coast Guard plant more than 250 red mangrove propagules

By Zoila Palma: On July 29 2026, the Belize Forest Department, in partnership with the Belize Coast Guard planted over 260 red mangrove propagules at the Coast Guard Headquarters in recognition of the International Day for the Conservation of the Mangrove Ecosystem.

The Belize Forest Department says that this restoration effort also forms part of the Greening Belize Initiative, our national commitment to restoring degraded ecosystems, increasing forest and mangrove cover, and building resilience to climate change through collaborative action.

The Forest Department extended appreciation to David Hilmy for his generous support in supplying the mangrove propagules and for assisting in making this initiative a success.

World.title: International News: Union of European Football Associations threatens World Cup boycott over FIFA plan to sell stakes
World.content:
International News: Union of European Football Associations threatens World Cup boycott over FIFA plan to sell stakes

By Zoila Palma:European football’s 55 national associations have unanimously rejected FIFA’s proposal to allow private investors to acquire stakes in a new commercial subsidiary overseeing the sport’s major competitions, warning that they could boycott FIFA tournaments if the plan is approved.

The decision was reached during an emergency virtual meeting chaired by UEFA President Aleksander Čeferin, BBC reports.

The potential boycott would cover FIFA competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cups and the Club World Cup, with the first possible test coming in October during the Women’s World Cup play-offs.

In a statement, UEFA said its members “stand as one” in opposing the proposal, declaring that the World Cup “cannot be treated as an investment product” and insisting that “the World Cup is not for sale.” The Football Association also said England stands “shoulder to shoulder” with its European counterparts and fully supports UEFA’s position.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino has proposed creating FIFA Forward Enterprise, which would allow third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments in the entity.

World.title: Belize leads Central American Commission for Environment and Development as first Technical Meeting on Seas and Biodiversity gets underway
World.content:
Belize leads Central American Commission for Environment and Development as first Technical Meeting on Seas and Biodiversity gets underway

By Zoila Palma: Belize, through the Ministry of Sustainable Development and Climate Change, is currently holding the first technical meeting of the Central American Commission for Environment and Development (CCAD) Technical Committee on Seas and Biodiversity, as the country serves as Pro Tempore President of the regional body.

The two-day meeting, which began on July 28 and is being held in a hybrid format, brings together technical specialists from environment ministries across the SICA region.

Discussions are focused on following up on ministerial agreements and advancing the committee’s work plan, with key topics including the state of biodiversity in the region and progress toward the goals of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

Participants are also reviewing the progress of the Subregional Biodiversity Center (CBD-CCAD), as well as the status of private reserves and wetlands throughout the SICA region. The meeting provides an opportunity for regional experts to exchange information and strengthen cooperation on the conservation and sustainable management of biodiversity and marine ecosystems.

The specialists are also receiving updates on several regional initiatives, including the Basin to Sea-CAM project, an integrated ecosystem conservation model supported by JICA, and biodiversity initiatives under the Great Forests of Mesoamerica and Linking Central American programmes.

World.title: Support for students
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith (right) confabs with Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia Grange at the post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House Wednesday, where Johnson Smith updated the nation on the situation with Jamaican medical students in Cuba.Garfield Robinson

THE Government of Jamaica has pledged continued support for the roughly 270 Jamaican students still studying in crisis-hit Cuba, with Foreign Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith reaffirming the Government’s commitment to the students’

welfare.

Johnson Smith told a post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House Wednesday that her ministry has been closely monitoring the students who remain in Cuba, 40 of whom are sponsored by Cuban scholarships, which are supported by the Government of Jamaica, further noting that one private student has formally advised of his return home.

Meanwhile, she noted that more than 65 students, including five on government scholarships, have completed their medical studies for the 2025-2026 academic year.

“Three others have indicated that they are in the process of continuing their studies elsewhere through academic transfer, and we have to caveat these numbers because we understand anecdotally that others have returned, but they have not formally notified us,” Johnson Smith said.

“And this is understandable, they are there privately, and on their own steam, but just to say that we have the information…and we also have a line of communication that allows for them to not only indicate their return, but to request assistance if they so need,” said the minister.

Johnson Smith noted that those students who remain are offered pathways to repatriation should they express a desire to return.

“This is because our concern remains for their safety, well-being, and academic continuity. We know that prolonged power cuts and reduced public transportation causes challenges for their way of life, and the Government has communicated our preparedness to assist with one-way return tickets should they wish to return but have a difficulty with affordability,” she said.

“We continue to engage the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Finance, and the Ministry of Health, as well as medical tertiary institutions on what, if anything, can be done for those who may wish to return and continue their studies here,” she added.

Many of the Cuban medical students have seen classes suspended or moved online with limited connectivity, as Cuba faces an ongoing energy crisis, worsened by a United States blockade on fuel shipments.

The island’s fuel shortages have been triggering frequent, lengthy, and unpredictable electricity interruptions, affecting not only education but also access to food, medical supplies, and transportation.

Back in February, Johnson Smith said some students had been reaching out and advised that their institutions either closed for a period, in one case for four weeks; and others said that classes had been suspended in favour of virtual studies, which saw challenges with Internet and electricity.

To maintain direct contact, Johnson Smith noted the ministry created a WhatsApp group, at that time linking roughly 320 students with officials in Kingston and the Jamaican Embassy in Havana, a move that allowed the Government to register many privately funded students who were previously outside formal channels.

In the meantime, Johnson Smith said Wednesday that the Government has reaffirmed its commitment to Cuba by contributing US$100,000 through the Caribbean Community (Caricom) as a humanitarian relief effort.

She said Jamaica joined Caricom heads of Government in continuing to express deep concern over the worsening humanitarian situation in Cuba and reaffirmed its commitment to a coordinated regional response to provide humanitarian assistance to the Cuban people.

“While speaking as long-standing friends of both the United States and Cuba, Caricom underscored in our joint single statement that civilian needs must remain the highest priority. We welcomed recent rounds of discussions between the governments and continue to advocate for constructive dialogue as the most effective path to relieve hardship on the people of Cuba,” said Johnson Smith.

The minister added that many Cuban medical professionals who had left the island following an abrupt end to the long-standing health technical cooperation arrangement in March 2026 have since returned to Jamaica and are continuing work under new arrangements with the health and wellness ministry. Johnson Smith added that those who chose to remain are still being accommodated as they continue to work under individual contracts.

“We all continue to value the significant contribution that Cuban medical professionals have made to our health sector over many years, and following the conclusion of the technical cooperation programme, you’d recall that a number of Cuban medical professionals chose to remain in Jamaica and continue to work under personal contracts,” she said.
