World.title: Army to use blood tests to detect brain injuries from weapon blasts
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDefence Army to use blood tests to detect brain injuries from weapon blasts Matthew Knott July 30, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Up to 400 Defence Force personnel will be tracked during weapons training as part of a sophisticated study that follows years of growing complaints about a lack of action on alarming reports of blast injuries among military veterans. In the first-of-its-kind study, researchers will cross-reference blast pressure readings from gauges on soldiers’ helmets with blood tests and neurological data conducted within a day of exposure to blasts. Retired lieutenant colonel Paul Scanlan, an advocate for action on blast injuries in defence, during his time in the army. Blood tests analysed at Monash University’s Melbourne laboratory will be used to detect tiny amounts of proteins known to be released in the bloodstream during a traumatic brain injury. The study is a response to the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide, which recommended the government establish a brain injury program to better understand the impact of repetitive low-level blast exposure on brain processes.



Retired army lieutenant colonel Paul Scanlan has led a veterans’ push for greater action from government and the Australian Defence Force on brain injuries among current and former service personnel. “From Afghanistan, there are guys now from that who have committed suicide,” Scanlan previously told this masthead. “And not just suicides. Families are being destroyed because of the effect it’s having. I think they deserve a lot better.” Veterans Affairs Minister Matt Keogh said: “The health, safety and wellbeing of current and former serving Defence Force personnel is my highest priority. “As part of our response to the royal commission, we’ve been investing in research and monitoring to better understand the complex nature of brain injury and its causes.



“While a co-ordinated effort is under way to decrease risks where possible, in line with international research, we know we need to do more.” In a 2024 interview with this masthead, then-army chief Simon Stuart apologised to veterans suffering from potentially avoidable impacts of blast trauma. Related Article Exclusive

Investigations The blasts, the battle and at last an apology. Now it’s time for action “There have been research and trials and other work going on since 2010, so far as I can ascertain. I think what’s been missing is sort of the golden thread of logic,” he said. Previous ADF studies have recorded blast pressure via the helmet-mounted gauges, but have not cross-referenced the results with blood and neurological data to determine the actual effect of blast pressure in real time.



Professor Sandy Shultz, a principal investigator at Monash’s school of translational medicine, said: “There has been very little research on brain injury as a result of low-level blast exposure, despite this being such a common experience across the defence sector. “Exactly how and to what extent low-level and repetitive exposures to blast affects the brain is really unknown. “The knowledge gained from this research will help inform policy and guidelines around what thresholds can result in a brain injury and when ADF personnel should be removed from further exposure.” The study, which will be conducted over the next four years, will focus on how repeated, low-level blast exposures may impact brain health across a military career. More is known about high-level blast events, which can result in immediate traumatic brain injury.



The study will focus initially on the army but could later be extended to the navy and air force. “By combining blast monitoring, blood-based biomarkers and cognitive and psychometric assessments, we’re building the evidence needed to strengthen force health protection,” said army neurologist Lieutenant Colonel Antony Sutherland, a member of the study team. The royal commission, released in 2024, found that traumatic brain injuries are associated with a heightened risk of death by suicide in veteran and civilian populations. “Traumatic brain injury from blast exposure is common in active-duty military personnel,” the final report found. “Many researchers believe that the pressure wave passing through the brain significantly disrupts brain function, causing damage.”



The royal commission found current and ex-service members “reported receiving insufficient support from the ADF for brain injury and having difficulty obtaining compensation”. If you are a current or former ADF member or a relative and need counselling or support, contact the Defence All-Hours Support Line on 1800 628 036 or Open Arms on 1800 011 046. World.title: Solar recommendations could speed up installations, lower household bills - industry
World.content:
New recommendations for solar power could speed up installations and lower household bills, the industry says.

Minister for Regulation David Seymour laid out 15 recommendations to streamline solar uptake in a review published on Thursday.

He also advised legalising plug-in solar, which is currently illegal in the country due to concerns over electricity and fire risks.

"You may have heard people say in Australia you can go to Kmart, buy a plug-in solar panel, plug it in and be going just as though you'd bought a PS2 or a Sega Megastation, or any other device for that matter.

"However, this is much better for the environment and you actually make money instead of wasting your childhood," said Seymour.

Electrification advocates Rewiring Aotearoa welcomed the recommendations.

Its policy director Dave Karl said the suggestions addressed the challenges stopping households from taking up solar: delays and unnecessary added costs.

"I think absolutely solar's day has come in New Zealand and I think the commitments from almost every party around the finance through the ratepayers assistance scheme, will absolutely unlock the choice for more than 90 percent of households to get solar on board."

Rewiring Aotearoa policy director Dave Karl. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said the review cut through red tape without sacrificing safety: accredited installers employing properly certified electricians would still be required.

"I do see it as a job creation opportunity in the medium to long run, and I really hope some parties come out with good policies around building that workforce domestically," he said.

He said legalising plug-in solar would make it very popular with renters.

"And I think more so than just plug-in solar, we'll be seeing lots of people also pairing that with plug-in batteries, enabling them to capture cheap electricity overnight and use that a little bit during the day as well.

"So I think it'll be, I mean, not as game-changing for power bills as rooftop solar can be, but shaving 50 bucks, 20 bucks - everything counts these days for a lot of families."

Future Energy co-founder Heath Coleman agreed this was a positive direction for the industry.

"I think we're all very supportive to see the removal, making solar easier and faster for homeowners to get solar, ultimately, at the end of the day," he said.

But he said the biggest challenge was the workforce.

"What we're facing at the moment is that there's a long process to get registered and solar installers to have the micro credentials that they need in order to sign off and install a solar system."

A home powered by solar. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said apprentices in his team of 80 would have to wait an extended period of time after their qualifications before being allowed to install solar.

"We're really struggling to find people that have the right skill sets there because it's still a very new and emerging industry. So, we have to train people up constantly and that takes time and obviously a lot of cost in there as well."

He said he wanted to see the certification process speed up.

However, he said he thought the upfront costs would still be a major deterrent - even with rate payers assistance schemes announced by several political parties.

"I think financially all the numbers do tend to stack up'" he said.

'Significant savings'

But Consumer NZ's power switch manager Paul Fuge said solar installations typically took less than a decade to pay themselves back.

"The other way to look at it is in terms of the unit price.

"So currently the average price in New Zealand is around 35 cents to 40 cents a kWh, depending on where you live. And solar is coming in around 15 cents, including the cost of capital.

"So there's significant savings in terms of the cost of the electricity that's coming off a solar system compared to buying it from the grid."

Consumer NZ' power switchmanager Paul Fuge. Supplied / Consumer NZ

The consumer champion said the perceived hassle and expense of solar deterred consumers.

"I mean, this review is really about removing unnecessary barriers. And if these reforms make solar quicker and easier to install without compromising safety, that's a win for consumers," he said.

He also welcomed legalising plug-in solar, as renters would be able to reap the benefits too.

"But what we'd say is installation is only half the story," he warned.

Fuge said he wanted to see more oversight of buy-back rates - the price of selling electricity back to the grid.

"Consumers also need to get fair pricing and fair returns from the electricity they generate from their solar systems."

James Scott from Electrify the Hutt, a community-led initiative to promote electrification, said allowing solar panel companies to sign off on an installation without an inspection would help speed up the process, but there was also a need for more installers to meet the demand.

The Ministry for Regulation said a small-scale solar system could involve up to six different sign-offs and five site visits from four different entities before it could be switched on.

James Scott from Electrify the Hutt. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Scott said his daughter and son-in-law had to wait around seven weeks due to the amount of red tape.

However, Scott added that he was able to be connected within 48 hours as his installer had done the preparatory work.

"I think that the regulatory review is one part of it, and taking away some of those things will help," he said.

"I think the other thing... is we need a good supply of trained and competent installers who know what they're doing."

Scott said some solar panel companies had more business than they could cope with.

World.title: Is Australia losing its shine?
World.content:
A promise of a better life in Australia has drawn many New Zealanders across the Tasman in recent years. But economists say the tide may be about to turn.

As the economy slowed after the post-Covid boom, the number of New Zealanders migrating to Australia picked up. There was a net migration loss of 28,500 people to Australia in the year to December last year, smaller than the 31,100 in 2024 but much higher than the 3000 a year that was normal between 2014 and 2019.

The record was a loss of 43,700 in the year to March 2012.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said people were drawn to Australia because the country was richer and had become steadily more so than New Zealand for the last 40 years.

Australia's GDP per person started to diverge from New Zealand's in the 1970s and is now significantly higher.

What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

Eaqub said that was partly because of their commodity prices and a better terms of trade but it was not only mining that helped. New Zealanders were earning less on average and spending more of their income on housing.

But he said where New Zealand's house price relative to GDP per person, and rents relative to GDP had been higher for a long time, they were starting to converge.

"For a long time, New Zealand's housing market has just been really terrible in terms of how unaffordable it is, both in terms of house prices and rents… we spend a lot more of our income on housing compared to Australia, everything else is much the same.

"Ours has got a little bit better and theirs has got a lot worse."

Eaqub said the current slowdown in Australia's housing market could change the picture again but New Zealand had made more progress with its conversation about public policy and housing in recent years than Australia had.

"I'm not saying we're perfect but I think it's far more mature here than it is over there."

He said Australia's economy also had headwinds and unemployment rising, which might discourage people from moving there if their access to welfare was likely to be limited. Australia also has higher central bank interest rates with similar levels of inflation.

A comparison of house prices relative to GDP per capita in Australia and New Zealand from 1995 until 2025. Supplied / Simplicity

BNZ chief economist Mike Jones agreed there were signs that "some of those economic relativities are starting to tilt more towards New Zealand".

"Probably more so from the Australian side as the Aussie economy slows down. Household spending growth there is entering a softer patch alongside falling house prices and a likely further rise in unemployment. As an example, New Zealand job ads have been, tentatively, rising against a flat-to-lower trend in Australia. That's historically quite a good indicator to suggest some narrowing in the big gap between New Zealand and Aussie unemployment rates is likely. That subtle shift in labour market relativities is I think one of the key reasons why New Zealand departures to Australia have slowed up a little."

He said he would still frame it more as New Zealand catching up rather than overtaking.

"Australia's economy starts from an outright stronger position in nearly all areas. Our forecasts do have New Zealand growth catching up and eventually overtaking that of Australia over the next 12-18 months, but it could be quite a while before New Zealand's unemployment rate falls down to where Australia's resides in the mid-to-late 4s."

ANZ senior economist Miles Workman said the two economies had been on different paths for a while.and New Zealand had more of a "boom-bust" Covid experience than Australia.

"That's likely to remain the case for a while yet, with New Zealand starting from a weaker position than Australia in terms of economic momentum, meaning the hurdle to growth in New Zealand should be a bit lower. The starting point for the respective housing markets is a similar story.

"The difference in unemployment rates between Australia and New Zealand helps explain the trans-Tasman migration cycle. Our forecasts have that gap narrowing from late this year, which should reduce some of the incentive to move purely for cyclical labour market reasons.

"However, it will take more than a few years of business cycle divergence to address the more structural income differential between the two countries. Even if New Zealand's economy outperforms Australia's for a period, skilled workers will likely still be able to earn materially more in Australia doing similar work. Australia's labour market is also larger, with more major cities, industries and career opportunities to choose from."

He said it was possible New Zealand would start to look more attractive over the next little while, because it was coming off a weaker base.

"Closing the gap with Australia in a more structural sense would require stronger productivity growth over the long run, which is what ultimately drives higher incomes. A cyclical upswing alone is unlikely to be enough."

Westpac senior economist Satish Ranchhod last year argued that New Zealand's economic growth was likely to outpace Australia's.

World.title: FMA delivers offset loan warning for banks
World.content:
New Zealand's financial regulator is warning banks that offer offset mortgages to take notice of action in Australia.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) said its review had found customers might have been unknowingly paying more interest than they should because some banks had failed to properly manage offset accounts.

ASIC reviewed the offset practices of eight banks, representing more than 70 percent of Australia's A$2.5 trillion home loan market.

What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

It said, while practices varied significantly across the banks, it found weaknesses in how all banks set up, monitored and managed offset accounts, resulting in some customers missing out on promised savings.

Australian banks are the parent companies of Westpac, ANZ, ASB and BNZ.

Michael Hewes, director of deposit taking, insurance, advice and credit at the Financial Markets Authority, said it was encouraging banks in New Zealand offering offset products to consider ASIC's findings and reflect on the robustness of their controls to prevent similar harms impacting their customers.

"The Conduct of Financial Institutions regime requires Financial Institutions, including banks, to treat customers fairly and have effective policies, processes, systems and controls in place to do so. Additionally, the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act requires lenders to provide clear disclosure of loan terms and to charge reasonable fees and interest.

"Our monitoring of financial institutions includes looking at the products they offer. One of our current regulatory priorities is focused on product design, ensuring that, when developing new products or redesigning existing ones, financial institutions prioritise consumer needs while also considering the capabilities and limitations of their systems and processes.

"This follows thematic monitoring we undertook last year which highlighted the risks posed by legacy systems and a reliance on manual controls."

He said the FMA had previously taken action when financial institutions had failed to deliver products as promised.

World.title: Labour considered most capable of managing New Zealanders' top five concerns - survey
World.content:
The Labour party is considered most capable of managing all of the top five concerns for New Zealanders - including the economy, the latest Ipsos Issues Monitor has revealed.

National leads on just one of the top 20 issues: crime/law and order.

The quarterly survey asks 1000 New Zealanders what they think are the three most important issues facing the country, and the political parties they believe are most capable of handling them.

The monitor showed New Zealanders' assessment of government performance remained low, with an average rating of 4.1 out of 10 (compared to 4.2 in May).

Less than a quarter of respondents rated the government's performance positively (that is, between 7-10 out of 10) compared to 27 percent in May.

Rating of government performance over six months. Supplied / Ipsos Issues Monitor

The top five issues

The cost of living (62 percent) remained the top concern since May's survey, and healthcare/hospitals (38 percent) was still considered second most important, though it's been slowly trending downwards.

National's perceived ability to manage healthcare weakened significantly, reaching its lowest point since February 2024, while Labour's at its highest level in nearly five years.

The economy (34 percent) held at third place, but Labour overtook National as the party best placed to manage it - spiking from 28 percent in May to 34 percent in July, while National dropped from 33 percent to 30 percent.

The political parties seen as most capable of managing issues. Supplied / Ipsos Issues Monitor

Labour also took a decent lead in the perception of its ability to tackle housing (22 percent) - ranked the fourth most important issue.

Unemployment (20 percent) returned to the top five concerns, reaching a level last seen in late 2020 and overtaking concerns about petrol prices.

The report said it surveyed people during the announced ceasefire in the US-Iran conflict, which drove a sharp decline in concern about fuel, dropping it from the fourth most important issue to seventh equal.

Other trends

Labour is considered best placed to tackle 15 of the top 20 issues.

The political parties seen as most capable of managing other issues. Supplied / Ipsos Issues Monitor

The Greens are most trusted with climate change as well as environmental concerns, National with law and order, and Te Pāti Māori with issues facing Māori.

National and Labour are rated the equal best parties to take care of defence / foreign affairs.

The only issue that saw a significant increase in concern was race relations/racism, at 6 percent, placed 13th equal - up from 16th equal in May.

The study was conducted using online research panels between 8 and 14 July 2026, with 1002 New Zealanders aged 18 and older taking part.

World.title: 'He was a dictator': Mother of Marokopa children speaks out about her relationship with Tom Phillips
World.content:
By Mihingarangi Forbes and Annabelle Lee-Mather for Mata Reports.

For most people, the Tom Phillips case began when he first disappeared with his children into the bush in 2021 and ended when he was shot dead by police last year.

But for the children's mother, Cat Christey, the saga stretches back many more years, through a volatile and sometimes violent relationship - and the nightmare she's experienced continues.

In her first interview since her children were recovered from the bush, Cat told Mata Reports: "I would like to see anybody else endure what I have endured for all these years.

"People think that this started … when Thomas abducted the children the first time. This started long before that. This has been going on for a long, long time."

'There was no room for compromise'

As she still deals with agency meetings and the fallout from the dramatic end to Phillips' time on the run, Cat has spoken out about the difficulties of her relationship with him and the toll it has taken.

"He was a good provider but very controlling. It was a very... imbalanced relationship. His views on what a marriage should be were different to my own. We should have been a team. But there was no room for compromise; it was his way or the highway.

"And he liked to be in control, he was a dictator."

For most people, the Tom Phillips case began when he first disappeared with his children into the bush in 2021 and ended when he was shot dead by police last year - not for Cat Christey. RNZ / MATA

Phillips first took the couple's three children into the bush near Marokopa in the western Waikato in September 2021 without telling Cat where he was going. They were separated at the time.

He returned several weeks later, but then, in December 2021, he went bush with the children again.

Phillips remained a fugitive until he was killed in a shoot-out with police following a ram-raid in Piopio.

Cat says that during their relationship, Phillips "wasn't extremely violent" although she described slaps and how he once strangled her.

But she was more concerned about his psychological abuse.

"He would control all the finances, he would take vehicle keys away from me … he would control who I saw and when I saw them."

Cat describes a volatile and sometimes violent relationship. RNZ / MATA

A fascination with guns

She says Phillips had a fascination with guns and that at one point, she twice rang 111 to tell the police about it. However, she says, Phillips took the phone off her and hung up both times. "I truly believed police would show up because it was a 111 call … but police did not come."

Phillips ordered her out of the house after that incident. Although he later begged her to come back, Cat says she wouldn't.

A few days later, he began proceedings against her and the situation spiralled over the next few years.

Cat says Tom Phillips had a fascination with guns. RNZ / MATA

Cat found out about the shooting and the discovery of her children after police had first told a Netflix documentary crew - a documentary she says she told the officer in charge, Detective Inspector Andrew Saunders, that she objected to.

"I was dead set against it when they first told me. It was very blunt and I said they do not have my permission.

"[Saunders] told me they didn't need my permission, that they were just letting me know."

Cat says she objected to a Netflix documentary about the case. RNZ / MATA

Not a victim

It's one way in which she says she feels like she has been disregarded by police throughout the case.

For instance she says that she only found out through the media about the fact the police had decided not to charge anyone with assisting Phillips while he was on the run and that the case was no longer being actively investigated.

Also, she says, she was declined support for counselling because she was not considered a victim of crime.

"I had reached out to Victim Support … in the hopes that they might be able to assist with some sessions with my psychologist."

Cat feels like she has been disregarded by police throughout the case. RNZ / MATA

Cat says Victim Support spoke to the police about her situation but was told nothing could be done.

"Police refused to do a referral stating that we're not victims of crime." This was because what had happened to her was not considered domestic violence, a point disputed by Auckland University associate professor of law Carrie Leonetti.

"This abduction, I think, was an act of child abuse, but it was also an act of domestic violence against these children's mother," says Leonetti.

"Taking children and saying, 'You will not see them for three years, they will live or die depending on what I decide' is an act of domestic violence."

Cat was told Victim Support spoke to the police about her situation but was told nothing could be done. RNZ / MATA

Even Police Minister Mark Mitchell, who would not comment specifically about police actions, said he personally believed Cat was a victim.

"Any right-minded person would say that a mother, regardless of the circumstances, when they're separated from their children, and they've through the tragedy that we all saw unfold in front of the country, a lot of people would probably consider her as much a victim in terms of what has happened," Mitchell told Mata.

"But I cannot talk to the police response other than saying, in my experience, police are very, very good at making sure they identify, communicate and support [victims] as much as they can."

Police Minister Mark Mitchell said he personally believed Cat was a victim. RNZ / MATA

Agencies respond

In response to questions from Mata Reports about Cat's treatment and allegations, Detective Inspector Ross McKay said: "A number of the matters you are asking about are subject to the government inquiry into the disappearance of the Phillips children, and it would therefore be inappropriate for us to comment at this time."

A spokesperson for Manaaki Tāngata Victim Support said the organisation could not comment on individual cases, but added: "The Victims Assistance Scheme, which Victim Support administers on behalf of the Ministry of Justice, has specific eligibility criteria.

"Our Support Workers carefully consider each person's circumstances and identify the support available to them."

A public inquiry was tasked with considering whether government agencies took all practicable steps to protect the welfare and safety of the children. RNZ / MATA

A public inquiry into the disappearance of Phillips and his children has been delivered to Attorney-General Chris Bishop.

The inquiry, led by the Honourable Simon Moore KC, was set up under the orders of the previous Attorney-General, Judith Collins, and tasked with considering whether government agencies took all practicable steps to protect the welfare and safety of the children.

Bishop says the report will be presented to Parliament once the government has considered the recommendations and how to deal with suppression orders that are in place in the High Court and Family Court.

World.title: Paid firefighters to strike for one hour at midday on Friday
World.content:
Firefighters will be walking off the job for the 50th time since bargaining with Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) began in 2024.

Members of the New Zealand Professional Firefighters Union (NZPFU) will go on strike for one hour, from 12pm to 1pm, on Friday.

Secretary Wattie Watson said their members had not had a pay increase since July 2023.

That is despite FENZ having offered an increase of 2.4 percent for non-union members earlier this month.

Watson said it was an unprecedented level of industrial action in New Zealand, but was needed due to union busting and retaliatory action from FENZ.

In a statement, deputy national commander Megan Stiffler said it remained focused on achieving a fair and sustainable settlement with the NZPFU, "so we can continue working to keep communities safe".

Watson said the only offer made by FENZ was in July 2025, which offered 2 percent for 12 months from the date a deal was ratified, and 1.5 percent for each of the two following years.

However, Stiffler said the offer would have had a 2.2 percent increase from December 2025, and 2 percent from January 2027 over a 24-month term to the end of November 2027.

The offer would have cost $50 million over four years, Stiffler added, whereas NZPFU's settlement proposal was for more than $130m over the same period.

"We continue to call on the NZPFU to call off these reckless strikes while we remain engaged with the Employment Relations Authority (ERA) to try and come to a resolution," Stiffler said.

Stiffler said the ERA had proposed both FENZ and the NZPFU to exchange their full revised bargaining positions at the same time, to help assess whether further facilitation was likely to assist, but NZPFU refused.

Watson said that NZPFU had been clear that it wanted to return to bargaining, but after more than 50 days of negotiations, there was no point unless FENZ was going to make a new offer.

FENZ to prioritise emergencies

FENZ warned that it would prioritise emergencies, and may not attend less serious incidents, during the one-hour strike.

Stiffler said all 111 calls would be received and responded to, and it had an arrangement with Hato Hone St John and the Wellington Free Ambulance for medical events in impacted areas.

"However, our response times will be delayed in impacted areas as volunteer crews will be responding from the next closest location. So, we are asking the public to remain extra careful."

World.title: Stephen Fleming replaces Brendon McCullum as England Test coach
World.content:
England has named Stephen Fleming as its Men's Test head coach, replacing one New Zealander with another.

He fills the space left by Brendon McCullum, who was fired earlier this month following a string of poor results and several off-field incidents.

In an announcement on Thursday night (NZT), the England and Wales Cricket Board also named Joe Root as returning captain.

Fleming, who played 111 Tests for New Zealand between 1994 and 2008, stepped down as Chennai Super Kings (CSK) head coach earlier this month after 18 years with the Indian Premier League franchise.

"Fleming is one of the most highly regarded coaches in world cricket," the board said.

"As a player Fleming was New Zealand's longest-serving (80 Tests) and most successful Test captain (28 wins). He played for Middlesex, Yorkshire and Nottinghamshire where also enjoyed success in captaining Notts to a drought-breaking County Championship title in 2005."

It said Fleming was chosen unanimously "following a rigorous process, which involved numerous high-quality candidates".

England's next series is against Pakistan next month. Marcus Trescothick will serve as interim head coach, with Fleming due to start in time for the winter tour to South Africa.

"This is to allow Fleming to spend time with his family in New Zealand after leaving his long-term association with CSK earlier this month. Fleming is set to fly to the UK later this summer."

Fleming said he was "incredibly excited" to be appointed to "one of the most prestigious coaching positions in world cricket".

"I am looking forward to working with the players and bedding in the gains made by Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes. Of course, the ambition is always to win now. But equally, it's about ensuring the team is well placed for the medium and long-term future. There is a lot of young talent in and around the team and our aim is to help them fulfil their potential as world-class cricketers," he said.

England’s captain Harry Brook (L) interacts with team head coach Brendon McCullum on March 4, 2026. PUNIT PARANJPE / AFP

"I'm particularly looking forward to working with Joe Root as Captain - a generational talent who has achieved so much already. There is still plenty more to come from him, and I'm excited to support him so he can enjoy and thrive in the role in what is a different context to his first stint.

"I'm also excited to work with Harry Brook. The best players are never finished products, and helping Harry continue to develop his extraordinary talent and his leadership will be an important part of this journey.

"I know what it feels like to have the weight of leadership and international cricket take their toll, and when that happened to me, my love for the game was rekindled by going to Notts and winning the County Championship. English cricket gave that to me and it is a privilege to have this chance to give something back."

McCullum, who played under Fleming in the Black Caps, will remain England's white ball coach and the pair will be required to work closely together.

World.title: Tomic continues resurgence, de Minaur sets up clash with Hewitt
World.content:
Born-again Bernard Tomic has continued his extraordinary renaissance with another stunning victory to surge into his first ATP quarterfinal in seven years.

A day after notching the fastest win on the tour all year, Tomic claimed the prized scalp of dual grand slam semifinalist Karen Khachanov in a straight-sets blitz in Mexico on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

And rounding out a banner day for Australian tennis less than a month out from the US Open, world number six Alex de Minaur has beaten his old nemesis Stefanos Tsitsipas to set up an intriguing showdown with Cruz Hewitt in Washington.

The day, though, belonged to the resurgent Tomic.

The one-time world number 17 crushed fourth-seeded Khachanov — the big-serving Russian who ousted Nick Kyrgios to reach the 2022 US Open semifinals — 6-2, 6-4 to continue his spectacular comeback from the brink of retirement.

The 33-year-old hinted he was considering hanging up his racquet before snaring the Lincoln Challenger this month.

"I'll be as honest as I can, about 10 days ago I hit a bit of a brick wall, maybe two weeks ago," Tomic said in the aftermath of his biggest breakthrough since 2018.

"I said this was going to be my last year, so I guess I have to reassess a few things now. Now that I won, I'm going to have to go back to the table. I'm probably going to play another 20 years."

Twenty more years may be a stretch, but Tomic is playing some vintage tennis.

The former teenage Wimbledon quarter-finalist only made the main draw in Mexico as a qualifying lucky loser.

Now he is three wins away from hoisting the trophy in Los Cabos, having earlier needed just 46 minutes to take down Alex Hernandez 6-1, 6-0 in the first round.

Currently ranked 171st, Tomic will climb even further and potentially to as high as number 132 if he wins a most unexpected fifth ATP title.

Next up will be either British fifth seed Cam Norrie or fellow Australian James Duckworth in Tomic's first ATP quarterfinal since losing to de Minaur in Atlanta in 2019.

De Minaur, meanwhile, is celebrating his own big victory, after downing Tsitsipas for only the second time in 14 meetings to reach the last 16 in the US capital.

The 6-4, 3-6, 6-3 win earned the top seed and defending champion a first-time encounter with 17-year-old Hewitt, de Minaur's understudy and son of Australian Davis Cup captain and mentor Lleyton.

After winning his first ATP match on Wednesday, Hewitt said it would be a "dream" to square off against de Minaur, who he likened to a big brother.

"I've known him basically my whole life," said Hewitt, who made the Wimbledon boys' final two weeks ago.

"​He's stayed with us and we have Christmas together, also. He's taught me so ​much. I think that ⁠would be a pretty cool memory for us."

AAP

World.title: Last-minute race to deliver marathon medals after shipping delays
World.content:
A last-minute logistical scramble has ensured thousands of runners at a major Queensland marathon festival will receive their medals.

A record number of more than 16,000 people will descend on the Sunshine Coast as the region hosts the event on Sunday.

But participants received an email late on Wednesday informing them they might not get a medal for crossing the line.

A medal from last year's Sunshine Coast Marathon Festival. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Event director Jason Crowther told the ABC a container full of T-shirts and medals arrived at the Port of Brisbane on Tuesday, but was stranded on the dock.

Mr Crowther said the merchandise was ordered months ago and was due to arrive on July 3, with the shipping company blaming point-of-origin delays and a typhoon for the late arrival.

"This is something you just don't want to happen," he said.

"To not get a finisher medal is not acceptable from our point of view.

"We don't take this lightly."

The Sunshine Coast Marathon Festival is a popular event, which attracts runners from around the country. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Marathon)

Port mobilises to solve crisis

When the Port of Brisbane was made aware of the issue following a media enquiry, officials rolled up their sleeves.

Executive general manager Brendan Connell said he was "really pleased" to help.

"We've been able to identify the container, get it moving and get it onto the Sunshine Coast so that all those hard-running marathoners, very worthy recipients, can get their medals on the weekend," he said.

"As soon as we found out … we wanted to do everything we could to help.

"We made a couple of phone calls, some senior people made some decisions, and in fact they disrupted their own days to ensure that we could identify this container.

"A few other things were put on the backburner to make that happen, but ultimately, everybody was able to come together and get to a really good outcome."

The event provides a much-needed tourism boost for the region over the winter months. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Marathon)

Mr Crowther said he was grateful to port officials for helping get the medals and merchandise released.

"They've moved heaven and earth to make it happen so a big thank you to them," he said.

" I've had a week of sleepless nights; it was something that was meant to arrive a long time ago. "

For anyone considering calling the port to get their parcel delivered faster, Mr Connell has bad news.

"It is a really complex series of events that moves freight around the world," he said.

"This isn't a scenario we could repeat every day, it isn't something that we can ordinarily influence.

"But certainly when there's a massive event like this going on … we wanted to make sure we could come together and do what we could to find those medals and get them on their way."

Last year, tourism officials estimated the Sunshine Coast race weekend generated about $10.5 million for the local economy.

World.title: Final frontiers drive Hazlewood in twilight years
World.content:
Josh Hazlewood has more boxes to tick in a stellar career after returning to peak fitness following several injury impacted years.

The 35-year-old Australia paceman, veteran of 76 Tests, has never won a series in India or England, two classic confrontations that loom large in the 20 Tests at least the team are set to play in the next 12 months.

Australia have not won an away Ashes series since 2001, while 2004 was the last triumph in India — well before any of the current squad were playing Tests.

Australian men's Tests in 2026/27 August 12-26: Two Tests vs Bangladesh

Two Tests vs Bangladesh October 9-31: Three Tests in South Africa

Three Tests in South Africa December 9-January 7: Four Tests vs New Zealand

Four Tests vs New Zealand January 21-February 23, 2027: Five Tests in India

Five Tests in India March 11-15, 2027: One Test vs England

One Test vs England June, 2027: World Test Championship final (potential)

World Test Championship final (potential) June-July, 2027: Five Tests in England

"The big series are obviously England and India. I haven't won in South Africa either, so there are a few boxes to tick off there, not just me, but this whole playing group," Hazlewood said.

"That's been a driving factor during this prep, it is in the back of your head, and in the months leading into it. They're real big Test series, all away against tough competition. Hopefully we get the job done."

Hazlewood's most recent setback in the Test sphere came when Achilles tendon and hamstring injuries cruelled any involvement in last summer's Ashes series.

Since then he has returned to the bowling crease with a bang, helping Royal Challengers Bengaluru win back-to-back IPL titles.

Hazlewood has been preparing with other members of the Australia squad at the National Cricket Centre in Brisbane ahead of two Tests against Bangladesh in Darwin and Mackay next month.

He said the "big days" of training in one location and without other playing commitments had been ideal.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

"Leading into other Test series and Test matches, you're playing T20, you're playing one-dayers, you're travelling, so it's tough to fit those bowling sessions in," he said.

"It's just trying to replicate a day in the field of Test cricket. It's bowling multiple spells in a day. It's bowling back-to-back days."

"This has been tailor-made for a Test match, which I think should work out well."

Hazlewood said it would be "tough" for any of the quicks in the squad to play every Test in the next year.

"Maybe a spinner," he quipped.

Hazlewood, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Scott Boland, Brendan Doggett and Michael Neser will all be vying for games.

Boland, who has been in sensational Test form, has been mostly overlooked when Hazlewood was previously available, but it need not be an either/or proposition.

"I think we've only played one game together … in England at Edgbaston, which was nice. I'd love to play more with Scotty," Hazlewood said.

"We're obviously a little bit similar, but there are still a lot of differences in our bowling. Every time he's come in, he's done unbelievably well. His career just keeps getting better and better the older he gets.

"I think there are enough opportunities in the next 12 to 18 months for us to play a lot of cricket, hopefully, together. We've got Ness (Neser) and Doggy (Doggett) there as well, so I think we'll have to lean on all six at some point in the next 18 months."

Hazlewood's most recent injuries have coincided with home Tests, but he is not sweating over what transpired in the past.

"We've got a nice lead-in this time. We've got Test matches abroad, so hopefully we hit the ground running again in Australia," he said.

"I've been lucky enough to play 70-odd Test matches now, which is quite a lot in terms of Aussie quicks. Hopefully I can tick a few more off."

AAP

World.title: People across Ireland wake up at all hours to watch AFLW
World.content:
In the middle of the night in a house in Ballinamore, in the North West of Ireland, Sharon O'Dowd wakes up to put on an Australian broadcast.

Two years ago, her young sister Eilish, who she helped raise with 12 years between them, moved from County Leitrim to Sydney to play AFLW for GWS.

Sharon and Eilish ODowd at a Gaelic game. (Supplied: Sharon O'Dowd)

When one of two of Eilish's matches haven't been available to stream across the ocean, the mother of two — her kids three and six — has put the commentary on and sat and listened instead while the rest of her house sleeps.

"I don't mind getting up this early as I love to watch her and the Giants play," Sharon told ABC Sport.

"If it's a particularly early game I usually go back to bed after it."

Sharon is one of many families across Ireland who wake up at all hours to watch GAA-turned-AFLW stars.

There are 47 Irish players in the AFL women's competition, many of whom will be on show in this weekend's inaugural AFLW Australia v Ireland clash in Sydney.

Their feats regularly make headlines back home.

Eilish with the first touch of her ball for GWS scored the fastest opening goal in AFLW history. The clip — in which she won the tap in the ruck and bolted straight through the corridor to score within 15 seconds — made the national news.

Sharon and EIlish O'Dowd. (Supplied: Sharon O'Dowd)

As it was her first game, Sharon was still getting familiar with the stream and watched, stunned, from her phone.

"I was in shock when she scored because I just couldn't believe what had happened," Sharon said.

"Everyone else in my house was asleep so I couldn't even celebrate with them. I knew my parents were watching the game in their house so I texted them.

"But it had happened so quickly they didn't even see it because they hadn't got logged into their streaming account fast enough."

Luckily, they have since watched the video of the replay multiple times.

Vikki Wall is a two-time premiership player with North Melbourne. (Getty: Josh Chadwick/AFL Photos)

Over in Dunboyne, a town of less than 10,000 people in County Meath, the Wall family regularly pack their house for North Melbourne games.

Tom and Caroline Wall's daughter, Vikki Wall, is a star sportswoman from the Eastern Coast.

She twice led County Meath to historic All-Ireland Senior Championship titles in 2021 and 2022 before being signed as an international rookie by North Melbourne and playing all 13 games of her 2022 debut season.

Vikki Wall is a star player in Ireland. (Supplied: Caroline Wall)

She missed the 2023 AFLW season to play rugby sevens for Ireland ahead of the Paris Olympics and returned to Arden Street to win premierships in 2024 and 2025.

"We've had events in our house where 30-plus people come and have breakfast and cheer on the teams," Tom told ABC Sport.

"We try to watch all of Vikki's matches but it can be difficult to access the games online sometimes, so we listen to the match commentaries on the radio, if necessary."

Like Sharon, this means getting up before the sun. "But it's worth it," said Tom.

Dublin, Ireland, August 15, 2021: Vikki Wall of Meath is congratulated by family following the TG4 All-Ireland Senior Ladies Football Championship Semi-Final match between Cork and Meath at Croke Park. (Getty: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile)

Vikki's younger sister Sarah was drafted to the Kangaroos last year. Thankfully for Tom and Caroline, this means still just the one early alarm.

Similarly, Collingwood's Sarah Rowe is a cross-code athlete, whose dad has followed her career across the globe.

Sarah represented County Mayo across all age groups from under-12 to the senior team before she moved to Australia.

There, she became a fan favourite for the Magpies after debuting in 2019 and won an A-League Women's championship with the Central Coast Mariners in 2025.

Her father Alan hasn't missed a game.

"My passion for the AFLW is total," Rowe told ABC Sport.

Sarah Rowe with her dad Alan after winning the A-League Women championship. (Supplied: Alan Rowe)

"I originally had not a clue about the rules, regulations or how to play the game but over a period of time, I've got to understand everything about it, I've seen the great players grow and understood the game passionately and very deeply, to now [to be able to] say that's it's one of the great games that I love watching."

Rowe has made the trip over to Sydney for the first AFLW Australia v Ireland representative game, as he does for all her big games: her 50th, 75th and Collingwood's 2022 semi-final against Adelaide.

"It's a great honour to represent the country at the highest level and I will be there with great pride and for the family and for the town of Ballina," Rowe said.

Alan Rowe hasn't missed a single game of his daughter's, Collingwood star Sarah Rowe. (Supplied: Alan Rowe)

Back in Ballina, Sarah's mother Grainne will be watching the match with "everybody within our family," Rowe said, including aunties, uncles and cousins.

"It's one of the big days of sporting life within the Irish calendar.

" And it'll be one that everyone will be so much looking forward to watching and very proud to be a part of. "

Sharon said it gets hard being away from Eilish, but she's happy players like her sister can give their all to the game overseas.

"When she has had a great game I would just love to be there to be able to tell her how amazing she is, and also when she is having a hard time or she gets injured I would love to be able to make sure she is ok. We do video calls all the time though so that helps," Sharon said.

The AFLW Australia v Ireland Cup and Best on Ground medal ahead of the inaugural clash. (Getty: Matt King/AFL Photos)

She's hoping it'll be a very happy FaceTime after Saturday's game against Australia at North Sydney Oval.

"It is an incredibly proud moment for all our family to see Eilish wear an Irish jersey and represent her country. There is no higher honour in sport in my opinion," she said.

"I'd imagine for this game the whole family will get up early to see her. We will have our Irish flags out and cheer the whole team on."

World.title: Storm coach responds to Munster's PNG ultimatum
World.content:
A part of Craig Bellamy would love it if he and Cameron Munster could bow out of Melbourne together.

But as the pair consider their NRL futures, Bellamy remains committed to supporting Munster whether or not he signs with expansion franchise PNG.

Storm veteran Munster turned the heat on Bellamy on Wednesday by claiming he would reject interest from the Chiefs for 2028 if Bellamy remained Melbourne's coach for that season.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

Bellamy re-signed with the Storm through 2028 in February, but the master mentor's diagnosis with a neurodegenerative condition has since cast doubt over his future.

On Thursday, Bellamy reiterated "the next year or two I'll be finishing up" but did not say whether his health would permit coaching on as late as 2028.

Bellamy handed Munster his NRL debut in 2014 and coached him in two premiership triumphs, with the 31-year-old now the Storm's longest-serving active player.

For Bellamy, the chance to bow out together would be fitting, but Munster indicated on Wednesday he may not be able to wait for the coach to make his own decision.

"I'd love to go right through my coaching career with him, ending about the same time," Bellamy said.

"[But] he's got a decision to make. He'll make the right decision for what's right for his family. He's got the right to do that.

"I'll back 'Mun' up, whatever he wants to do."

Munster remains sidelined with a knee injury for Friday's clash with resurgent Canterbury and is now joined on the pine by captain and hooker Harry Grant.

In a season of injury carnage, Bellamy said Grant's hamstring problem was another big blow for the 12th-placed Storm.

"Any team losing their captain, that's a big loss, but Harry especially," Bellamy said.

"He's always in the middle of the play whether it be with the ball or without the ball."

Injuries, roster turnover and a seven-game losing streak early in the season have all left the Storm's finals hopes hanging by a thread ahead of round 22.

A loss to the Bulldogs would ensure they miss the top eight for only the second time under Bellamy, and first since mass salary cap breaches consigned them to the wooden spoon in 2010.

It would also mark a 12th loss of the year — the most the Storm would have suffered in any of their 24 seasons under Bellamy.

"We know it's going to be a tough ask tomorrow night, but we've had a good week's preparation with the guys we've had," Bellamy said.

AAP

World.title: Cricketer dubbed 'Clicky Ponting' suspended as stats show unusual trend
World.content:
The club at the centre of the "Clicky Ponting" scandal in English amateur cricket has suspended its player over the matter.

Saltburn Cricket Club said Brian Devine had been suspended for the rest of the season after several videos were posted online with claims Devine was clicking his fingers as the ball passed the bat to mimic the sound of an edge.

The club has forfeited its next match in the North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League.

"We are treating this allegation with the utmost seriousness and, as a family-centric club, we are fully cooperating with the league's investigation," a statement read.

"We believe that the club acted decisively as soon as the complaint and investigation were made known to us.

"The player at the centre of the complaint has been suspended and will not play again for the club this season or in the foreseeable future, pending the outcome of this investigation."

Devine is yet to comment on the matter and an investigation into the claims has yet to be completed, with the allegations so far unproven.

However, an amateur data analyst on social media platform X said they had trawled all scorecards from Saltburn games and found wicketkeeper catches dramatically increased when Devine was playing.

"Been requested to split it by the matches where Devine (the slip clicker) played, and it's even more stark," X account @maxtempers, which usually posts about British politics, wrote.

"39 keeper catches in 13 matches with Devine. 5 keeper catches in 7 without."

The post followed an original analysis that found wicketkeeper catches increased four-fold when the particular keeper standing alongside Devine in the alleged clicking footage was playing, including eight catches in one innings.

The record at Test level is seven catches in one innings, shared by five players.

"The league has received a formal complaint regarding alleged incidents in a Division Two game on Saturday 25 July, 2026," a league statement read when the controversy came to light.

"A full investigation has been initiated and until such time as the formal processes are complete no further comment will be made."

Australian cricket podcasters The Grade Cricketer have offered to provide financial support to Devine and Saltburn.

World.title: Broncos premiership prop announces medical retirement due to blood clots
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos premiership prop Corey Jensen has announced his medical retirement from the NRL after ongoing problems.

Jensen, who played 95 games for Brisbane including last year's grand final win over Melbourne Storm, also played 58 games in five seasons for North Queensland.

After becoming unwell during round seven, Jensen was diagnosed with a pulmonary embolism (blood clots in the lungs).

"After receiving medical advice and speaking to specialists, it's clear that it's no longer safe for me to play rugby league," he told reporters.

Jensen said he had been told he would have to take blood thinners for the rest of his life.

Big Ben heading to NFL The Brisbane Broncos are releasing forward Ben Te Kura from the rest of his NRL contract to allow him to pursue his dream of playing in the NFL.

"Since [the diagnosis] I've been able to train properly again, it's been like a mini pre-season, and I can do everything other than the contact, which is the frustrating part.

"Overall, my health's pretty good, I can continue training in the future and it's not going to affect me in any way."

The Broncos had confirmed he had another incident with deep vein thrombosis in his calf a year earlier, with both incidents considered unprovoked, meaning there was no obvious trigger such as a long-haul flight or injury.

"I leave with absolutely no regrets," he said, thanking his teammates for being part of the premiership win with them.

"I never chased individual recognition, but being part of a team, seeing people grow and knowing that in some way I may have contributed."

Corey Jensen played 95 games for the Broncos after joining the Brisbane side for the 2022 season. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Jensen teared up, thanking his wife Shannen for all her support and the sacrifices she had made.

"People see the player, but they don't always see what partners give up behind the scenes," he said.

Jensen is a qualified sports scientist, having completed a Bachelor of Sport and Exercise Science at James Cook University, and will have a bright future in that space if he chooses to pursue it.

Jensen was not a star as a youth but, through hard work, turned himself into a weapon after debuting for the Cowboys in 2017 and playing in the grand final.

"The late Paul Green gave me my debut back then.

"I was a bit of a late bloomer, so I'm grateful they took a punt on me, and I have to acknowledge how much the Cowboys did for my career," Jensen said.

"Coming down here was kind of a kind of a new lease on life. The Broncos gave me the opportunity, and I'm eternally grateful for what this club's done for me both on and off the field."

ABC/AAP

Tech.title: ABC demands FCC drop its ‘punitive’ early license renewal of its stations
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

ABC filed its formal opposition to the Federal Communications Commission’s effort to force it to submit to an early renewal of its broadcast station licenses, calling it an effort to chill the speech of broadcasters across the country.

In a new filing with the FCC, ABC charges that the agency’s willingness to pursue the early renewal of eight of its licenses far before they expire is “extraordinary and unprecedented.” The company alleges the FCC “has spent the last 18 months searching for some pretext for revoking the Stations’ licenses,” but charges that the agency’s real motivations for pursuing these licenses are clear: “Each is owned by ABC, and the Administration has openly and repeatedly called for the revocation of ABC’s licenses, because it dislikes the content and viewpoints expressed on ABC network programs.” The FCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The FCC ordered ABC to file for early license renewal for the stations in April, noting that it had been investigating the company for potential violations of the law and FCC rules, “including the agency’s prohibition on unlawful discrimination,” an apparent reference to its probe into ABC and owner Disney’s Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) programs.

“The retaliation against ABC is a signal to every media company in the country”

The station license fight has led to an outpouring of support for ABC, including from viewers it urged with on-air ads to file public comments. More than 153,000 comments have been left on the FCC docket, including from a bipartisan group of former FCC chairs and officials who slammed the agency’s action as part of a “broader pattern” in a “campaign to punish speech disfavored by the Trump administration.”

The FCC under Republican Chair Brendan Carr has repeatedly targeted ABC for actions he claims violate their obligation as a publicly licensed broadcaster to serve the public interest. That included threatening the company’s licenses over a joke late-night comedian Jimmy Kimmel made on air after conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s killing, and attempting to penalize “The View” for platforming a Democratic candidate, positing it could be subject to equal time rules the agency previously ruled it was exempt from. Some of these actions have earned Carr criticism even from administration allies like Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX), who likened the chair to a “mafioso” over his threat over the Kimmel comments.

“The retaliation against ABC is a signal to every media company in the country: accommodate the Administration’s view of what news coverage should look like or pay the price,” ABC wrote in its latest filing. “The tools vary; the objective does not: a media industry too fearful of official reprisal to report the news freely.”

Tech.title: Google is working on Chrome updates that don’t require restarts
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google is working on a way to apply Chrome updates without requiring you to restart your browser. In a post on Thursday, Google outlines its approach to bug fixes in the age of AI, while noting that it’s trying to make updates less disruptive by “investing in ‘dynamic patching’ that will eliminate the need for a full browser restart.”

According to Google, AI-powered security tools have already helped the company find and fix dozens of bugs. Chrome 149 and 150, for example, contained 1,072 bug fixes, exceeding the number of patches in the past 23 major releases combined. That’s part of the reason why Chrome is switching to a two-week release cycle starting in September with security updates in between. However, Google says it’s considering introducing two weekly security updates to counter “fast-moving AI-powered attacks.”

To make these updates go more smoothly, Google is trying to “shift the burden away” from users, who could be at risk of “N-day” attacks, which occur when hackers exploit newly released bug fixes that haven’t yet been downloaded on a user’s device.

Along with working on dynamic patching, Google is also trying to find “opportune moments to restart automatically, when we can guarantee a seamless session restore.” Google has already launched a version of this in Chrome 150 on macOS, as the browser takes advantage of a state “where applications typically continue running in the background even after all windows are closed.” Chrome will automatically restart if it detects an update in this windowless state, Google says.

“Our long-term vision is a browser that is always up-to-date — continuously and dynamically patched, and automatically restarted during opportune periods of minimal disruption,” Google writes.

The renders also show the phone in an olive green color that I think looks really nice.

Tech.title: Friend re-launches its AI pendant with a speaker that talks to you, for twice the price
Tech.content:
is a technology reporter who has been covering the industry since 2007. He co-hosts the Waveform podcast with MKBHD. A former engineer, he now specializes in topics like computational photography and social media protocols.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Do you remember Friend? The Friend that launched an AI pendant, spent $1.8 million of its $2.5 million to acquire friend.com, and plastered the NYC subway with ads promoting artificial companionship?

Yeah well, if you didn’t remember, Friend is back. And now, it’s twice the price.

This morning, Friend launched a new ad showing two people talking to their Friend pendants about very personal life problems. It didn’t say it explicitly, but the ad showcased a new feature the pendant now includes: a speaker. Before, Friend would only message back to you, but now, it will talk to you, too. For some reason, the addition of that feature is apparently worth $120, as the originally $129 product now costs $249.

The re-launch comes about nine months after a large Friend protest took place in NYC, where protestors tried to bring attention to our growing dependance on technology. Friend was the obvious target, considering it had spend a boatload of money advertising throughout the city. Its founder, Avi Schiffmann, even posted an image promoting the protest, and showed up to it himself.

Shiffmann posted a tweet of the new ad, calling it “Friend 2.0,” even though the product is still just called “Friend” on its site. I’m sure things will go much better this time.

Tech.title: Best Buy is selling an RTX 5080 for more than the RTX 5090’s MSRP
Tech.content:
Best Buy has raised the price of the Asus ROG Astral RTX 5080 OC to $2,099 — the first time a major US retailer is directly selling an RTX 5080 for more than the $1,999 MSRP of the RTX 5090, VideoCardz reports. The ROG Astral RTX 5080 OC now costs 40 percent more than its launch price of $1,499, and over double the $999 MSRP of the RTX 5080 Founders Edition.

As VideoCardz notes, this is currently the only RTX 5080 directly sold by Best Buy that’s priced over the RTX 5090’s MSRP. There are still other RTX 5080 GPUs available for significantly less, including at other retailers — Asus is selling the ROG Astral RTX 5080 OC for $1,899, which is still more than its launch price but a bit lower than Best Buy. However, component shortages and RAM price hikes aren’t showing any sign of slowing down any time soon, so more RTX 5080 GPUs could see similar price hikes.

Best Buy’s price increase also follows reports that Nvidia is planning to increase its GPU prices by 20 to 30 percent, its third such price hike this year. With prices for RAM and other components rising, we’ve even seen the return of GPUs with 4GB of VRAM like the ASRock AMD Radeon RX 9050 Challenger.

Tech.title: Xiaomi’s SkyNomad N90 Max is an extended-range EV with a transforming interior
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

The SkyNomad N90 Max is the latest electric SUV from Xiaomi and its first extended-range EV, with a claimed range of over 1,705 km (about 1,059 miles). It will come in both five- and seven-seat configurations, as well as an N90 Max Camping Edition.

One of the big features of the N90 is its highly customizable interior. The front seats rotate 180 degrees, the center armrest slides out to become a small table, and the second row features zero gravity seats with footrests. The Camping Edition adds a pop-up top, a rooftop bed platform, an attachment point for a tent, and a detachable table. Some models will also include a fridge and overhead speakers. Xiaomi is pitching the N90 as a sort of living space on wheels, saying it can be a “studio for one, a cafe for two, a lounge for three, a playground for the whole family.”

Interior flexibility is the big selling point here. Image: Xiaomi
